#412. Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI

Scott Wiener has made AI regulation a cornerstone of his political career. Now he’s headed to Congress.

As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.

I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control.

“It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.”

Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.”

Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation.

Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry, but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth.

“Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.”

Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve. And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator.

He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what's going on,” he says.

And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says, laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.”

Above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says. That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over AI,” he told me. “We need to deal with recursive self-improvement. Once you’re in that realm, that really is potentially a recipe for total loss of control.”

He’ll have some allies in the fight against catastrophic AI risk. Senator Bernie Sanders, for instance, has met with many of the AI safety movement’s most influential figures and has spoken repeatedly about AI and existential risk. But there’s still a large gap between Wiener’s Bay Area, AGI-pilled perspective and the national mood on AI, which is anchored by opposition to data centers. The fact that voters approved 40 out of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on Tuesday might seem to be a good sign for Wiener and others who support AI regulation, but Wiener says he sees this movement as far more tied to local concerns than to bigger questions about AI risk.

“Peoople who are really opposed to where AI is going—this is an area where they can actually do something about it,” he says. “But the data center revolt—to me, I think it’s more so that people are upset that there could be something like this in their community, with all the impacts near people’s homes, driving up electric bills and using water. I think that’s the bigger issue for most people, from what I can tell.”

Wiener describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI, given its poor track record on regulating the tech industry. He also has concerns about the ability to get legislation past President Donald Trump, who called concerns about catastrophic AI risk a “hoax” in September and has demonstrated a stark unwillingness to collaborate with China, something that Wiener sees as essential to preventing the worst consequences of AI.

But he says Trump’s unpredictability provides  some measure of hope, though it’s a fraught kind of hope. “So far what we’ve seen are some problematic things, but not complete disasters,” Wiener says. “I hope that it doesn’t take a disaster to spur the president into acting. And I hope if that’s what it does take—which, like I said, I hope it doesn’t—but if it does, I hope it’s as small as possible.”

#408. The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity

Big Tech sees a culture war over progress. But the real fault line is electricity: drawing it from the grid and generating it onsite provoke different kinds of backlash, neither easily solved by public relations.

This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape.

Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ.

It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words.

But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity.

Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid.

One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables).

The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport.

Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity.

Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out.

Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand.

The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company.

Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid.

But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out).

The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale.

Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency).

Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do. But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation?

Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that.

But as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something.

So what happens next? It’s possible that newly elected politicians’ actual stances on data centers won’t be as negative as the ones they campaigned on. But what seems true regardless is that if new data centers need their own power generated onsite, they’ll go where there are the fewest people able to resist them. That might mean the Permian Basin, where a network of natural-gas lines can be easy for developers to connect to and populations are sparse. Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia.

But there’s one place where Big Tech may find virtually no limits at all, as Elon Musk posted just hours after the midterms results came rolling in: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

#407. Shania Twain calls for equal pay and more diversity in country music

Shania Twain is standing up for others in country music.

The legendary star in the genre used her acceptance speech for the Equal Play Award at Sunday’s CMT Awards to call for more equity and diversity in the country music industry.

“When I wrote the phrase ‘Man I feel like a woman’ I honestly had no idea at the time it would become an undercurrent of a decades-long career,” she said, referring to one of her biggest hits. “It’s amazing how one statement can empower so many.”

The phrase, Twain said, “has been adopted by an array of fantastic communities all around the world and become a genuine path of power…which brings me so much joy.”

“I believe in an all-inclusive country music. We’re family,” Twain said. “This is a genre of music with a rich history that raised and nurtured my own songwriting and performance and recording career from childhood. Currently, the industry standard does a real disservice to this.”

Twain, who was presented the award by rapper Megan Thee Stallion, shouted out some of the diverse acts she is spotlighting on her “Queen of Me” tour this year, including Lily Rose, Lindsay Ell, Hailey Whitters, Mickey Guyton and others.

“I will continue to do my best as a trailblazer,” Twain said. “Together, let’s ensure all our fellow artists get equal play regardless of gender, age or race.”

She also performed acappella with the African American singing group, The BoykinZ, while presenting an award onstage. Twain connected with the group, who are sisters and rising country stars, after Kelly Clarkson surprised them recently by bringing Twain out to meet them during an episode of Clarkson’s daytime talk show.

#405. The Polar Vortex Is About to Make Weather Weird From the UK to the US

A critical blockade against some of nature’s coldest air has temporarily broken down—and much earlier in the year than normal. Disruptions in this circulation, known as the polar vortex, often push intensely cold air out of the Arctic toward lower latitudes.

Experts still aren’t entirely sure how the current collapse will play out in our everyday weather. But it’s another sign that we may be in for a wild ride over the weeks and months to come.

The polar vortex is a band of upper-level winds wrapping around the Arctic Circle like a dam. This circulation is usually strong and stable, helping to keep the season’s coldest air locked near the North Pole. But the winds occasionally weaken or even reverse course, which can set off an atmospheric chain reaction, allowing bitterly cold air to spill southward.

The manner in which the polar vortex breaks down determines what kind of weather conditions we might expect. Upper-level winds dipping southward in troughs are responsible for brief spells of cold temperatures. These “lobes” of the polar vortex, as they’re known, are relatively common in a typical winter.

Sometimes, this circulation can splinter into smaller pieces. If the vortex were a flowing river, these fragments are like leaves stuck on the riverbank, forcing extremely cold air to linger over the same areas for days or weeks at a time.

One such case made this phenomenon a household name. A highly disrupted polar vortex in early 2015 sent a weeks-long burst of cold air sweeping over the eastern US. Chicago recorded its coldest February in nearly 140 years. In Lexington, Kentucky, temperatures bottomed out at –18 degrees Fahrenheit, as subfreezing air dove all the way to the Gulf of Mexico.

Seeing a breakdown of the polar vortex this early in the season is unprecedented in the historical record. Disruptions of this extent typically don’t occur until the latter half of winter. Based on the latest data, the circulation’s reversal began on Tuesday, and computer model guidance expects it to last through Thursday.

Weather patterns take a few weeks to respond to a polar vortex disruption, if at all. Given that reliable forecasts only extend about 10 days into the future, we can’t know where in the northern hemisphere cold air from the Arctic may spill.

While experts are still debating the exact causes driving this polar vortex breakdown, the event throws another wrench into a cool season already dominated by another unprecedented event: the strongest El Niño on record.

Historically warm sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific Ocean have already significantly affected conditions around the world, and this influence will only grow heading into the winter months.

Much of North America can expect warmer-than-normal conditions during a winter dominated by a strong El Niño. But every event is different, and now with a sudden disruption in the polar vortex, those forecasts are less certain, because unexpected things can happen when unprecedented phenomena overlap.

#403. Evolving metal extraction processes

Rethinking how metals are extracted could unlock lower-emission production, make better use of mineral resources, and strengthen critical-material supply chains.

The metals industry has experienced transformational moments before: the Bessemer process, flash smelting, electric arc furnaces, and modern continuous casting all changed what was possible.

Yet, for more than a century, most extraction processes rely on techniques and pathways that would be familiar to metallurgists from generations ago. Processes have become larger and control systems smarter, but the fundamental science behind separating metals from ores has changed less than many realize.

Today’s materials challenges are different from those of the 20th century, but why are critical metals still produced using largely the same scientific foundations?

EvoMaterials, a technology platform developed by Outokumpu—the global leader in sustainable stainless steel and the producer of ferrochrome with 67% lower carbon footprint than the industry average—is exploring that question by rethinking how metals can be extracted:

“We decided to go beyond the current constraints and look fundamentally at what’s the best way to do this with the benefit of the scientific engineering knowledge and hindsight that we have today,” says Caspar Stinn, technical director for extractive metallurgy at Outokumpu. “We’re looking at how we can reimagine metals production.”

As economies expand and the world becomes increasingly electrified, data and scientific models point to rising demand for many minerals, driven by technologies ranging from data centers to aerospace, water treatment, energy systems, and defence. According to Antoine Allanore, professor of metallurgy at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) this coincides with many Western economies having reduced their domestic processing capacity for the very metals those industries depend on.

Metallurgy is now strategically important, shaped not only by cost and availability but also by carbon footprint, geographic origin and supply-chain resilience.

That reality is particularly relevant for chromium and other specialty metals used in high-temperature and extreme environments. Chromium-based materials play a critical role in aerospace systems, power generation, corrosion-resistant infrastructure and defense technologies, where materials must perform under demanding conditions.

For decades, metallurgical innovation largely focused on improving yields, energy efficiency and process control. EvoMaterials is based on the idea that some metallurgical processes may benefit from entirely different chemical pathways.

The platform originates from research into sulfidation-based processing technologies, initially pursued to reduce carbon emissions associated with ferrochrome production. Laboratory work revealed broader potential.

Lab-scale trials demonstrated that these alternative process chemistries could potentially do more than lower emissions. They could recover valuable metals from lower grade resources and industrial side streams while fundamentally altering how separation processes are performed. The opportunity is to rethink how mineral resources are used and how much value can be extracted from them, bringing in greater resource efficiency and stronger industrial competitiveness.

Development of the technology began in the United States in 2021 for chromite from Outokumpu’s Kemi mine in Finland, the only chrome mine in the European Union and one of the few such operations across the Western world. Since then, Outokumpu has evolved the technology through extensive research and development, combining new process chemistries with proprietary metallurgical expertise, supported in part by a non-exclusive patent license agreement from MIT.

“The technology is a new application for separating metallic elements from materials,” explains Allanore. Historically, that separation has been achieved using carbon- and energy-intensive approaches. The new method creates a different chemical environment that enables more efficient extraction with fewer losses and fewer unwanted by-products, recovering critical materials from resources considered waste.

EvoMaterials sits at the intersection of several scientific disciplines, a combination that strongly resonates with Stinn, who completed his PhD in Materials Science and Engineering at MIT, where his research focused on low-carbon metals processing and recycling technologies.

Modern materials innovation draws on a growing mix of chemistry, materials science, physics, computational modeling, and engineering. With advanced simulation tools and AI helping researchers identify promising directions, scientific discovery still depends on experimentation and testing in the lab—on getting your hands dirty and doing the hard work.

“Science today is much more interdisciplinary than it was, and the collaboration across disciplines reveals new scientific opportunities,” says Stinn. Engineering can translate those opportunities into more efficient and cost-competitive metals production.

A technically significant aspect of EvoMaterials is that it’s not a single process, but a technology platform. Allanore compares EvoMaterials to platform technologies in other industries, where a single scientific breakthrough can enable multiple downstream applications.

Once a new extraction pathway has been mastered for one material system, the same scientific principles may be adapted to entirely different metals and mineral resources. The initial application becomes only the starting point.

“The future and the potential impact might be much broader than the original and current developments that are happening,” Allanore explains.

That possibility is increasingly important as industries seek secure supplies of nickel, chromium, molybdenum, and other strategic materials needed for advanced manufacturing.

The broader implication extends beyond metallurgy. Companies that develop proprietary process technologies may create value through production but also through intellectual property and scientific expertise.

Based on Outokumpu’s technology leadership, that transition could create entirely new categories of value, enabling the production of high-value critical materials from ores and resource streams that previously appeared uneconomical or inaccessible.

The result would be a fundamental shift in how metals are manufactured, where sustainability, resource efficiency, supply security, and economic value become outcomes of the same technological architecture rather than separate objectives.

The next step for EvoMaterials is pilot-scale validation, with a pilot plant in New Hampshire to begin operations in the first half of 2027. The facility will scale the proprietary technology from laboratory to one-ton production, providing a step toward industrial-scale deployment targeted for 2030. Beyond producing low-CO2, chromium-enriched ferrochrome and chromium metal, the platform could be adapted to other strategic materials, including nickel and molybdenum.

The work raises a broader question—how many of today’s metallurgical processes would look the same if they were invented from scratch? Or could those routes be designed differently today?

The next revolution in materials may begin by rethinking how to extract the metals that society depends on.

Read more about this topic and hear more from Caspar Stinn and Antoine Allanore.

#402. 2023 March Madness: Will UConn or San Diego State triumph in the national championship game that 'means everything?'

The University of Connecticut won its fifth men’s basketball national title with a 76-59 victory over San Diego State University on Monday night at NRG Stadium in Houston.

Senior guard Tristen Newton led UConn (31-8) with 19 points and 10 rebounds while Final Four Most Outstanding Player Adama Sanogo, a junior forward, chipped in with 17 points and 10 rebounds.

“We weren’t ranked going into the year so we had the chip on our shoulder,” UConn head coach Dan Hurley told game broadcaster CBS. “We knew the level that we could play at, even through those dark times,” he added, referencing the team’s six losses in eight games during the regular season.

He said going into the tournament his group had confidence garnered during the season.

“And when you have the type of leaders like Andre Jackson (game-high six assists Monday) and Adama Sanogo, they kept this team together, got us back on track and we knew we were the best team in the tournament going in and we just had to play to our level,” he added.

San Diego State (32-7) was topped by Keshad Johnson who had 14 points.

UConn trailed very early but San Diego State was undone by an 11-minute, eight-second stretch in which they scored just five free throws and missed 12 consecutive shots from the field. The Huskies went from down 10-6 to up 36-24 at halftime.

The Aztecs made a run midway through the second half and narrowed the deficit to five at 60-55 with 5:19 to play but the Huskies scored the next nine to take a comfortable lead into the final two minutes.

“We battled. Battled back to five in the second half, but gave them too much separation,” San Diego State coach Brian Dutcher said. “We had to be at our best. We weren’t at our best. A lot had to do with UConn.”

Senior guard Adam Seiko told reporters they gave themselves a chance with their second half comeback but UConn “just made a little bit more plays” at the end.

“They have a lot of weapons. They were pretty good,” said Matt Bradley, also a senior guard. “To beat them, we had to make shots. I shot poorly. And you had to have a really good game to beat those dudes on the offensive end.”

UConn won each of its six tournament games by at least 10 points, with its closest game being a 13-point win over the University of Miami in the national semifinals.

“I just want to thank my teammates, my coaches who believed in me. If it were not for them I would not be here right now,” Sanogo told CBS.

Jordan Hawkins, who scored 16 points for UConn, talked about winning the crown one day after his cousin, Angel Reese of Louisiana State University, won the women’s title.

“I mean it’s absolutely amazing that we both get this opportunity and I mean the family reunion is going to be great so that’s all I know,” he said.

UConn enters rarefied air as only the sixth team to win five NCAA men’s basketball championships, joining UCLA (11), Kentucky (eight), North Carolina (six), Duke (five) and Indiana (five). All of UConn’s titles have come since 1999 with the most recent before Monday occurring in 2014.

UConn’s women’s teams have won 11 basketball national titles.

CNN’s Steve Almasy and Issy Ronald contributed to this report.

#400. Rocco Classic Smart Fridge Review: A Cool Conversation Piece

Updated November 2026: The Rocco Super Smart Fridge is now called the Rocco Classic, after Rocco released two new fridges in 2026, the lower-priced Essential and desktop-sized Mini Mini. Copy has been updated to reflect the new moniker.

Opening up someone else’s kitchen refrigerator is an intimate act.

I for one would prefer my guests don’t go in there for a beer and see the raspberries that are probably moldy, revealing a dark side of my personality. I’ll just get their drink for them. Having a separate mini fridge just for drinks can help, and when I saw how fresh and innovative the Rocco seemed, I had to know more.

The Rocco Classic feels more like a piece of furniture sitting in my living room, as opposed to a regular mini fridge, which often looks like it’s out of a college dorm, or a more industrial-looking regular wine fridge. I have the matte graphite color (it also comes in white, green, brown, and mirror-black).

The whole thing is mostly made of steel, which makes it strong and heavy, and the rounded edges give it more of a soft appeal. It seems to be engineered very well, with quality materials, which I’m sure is why it costs as much as it does. This should last me a very long time in my home. Overall, it’s a beautiful statement piece that people who like to host in their home will love, but the features that make this a smart fridge are not perfect.

A typical wine fridge will generally fit full-size bottles of wine only, but the Classic can fit 77 12-ounce cans (though Rocco's website says 88) or 27 wine bottles in its 34.5 x 24 x 16-inch body (H x W x D). There are six shelves, each of which is designed so you can store bottles and cans of any size and stagger them to fit like a puzzle. Each shelf is also reversible so the grooves match whichever shape bottles you choose to place on each shelf.

The Rocco connects to an app on your phone (currently available only for iOS; Rocco hopes to have an Android version at some point). The app is simple and easy to use, but there aren’t that many things to do on it, and some of the features feel forced. First of all, there are a few modes you can control from the app. I keep mine on Quiet Mode. It really is extremely quiet. I rarely hear much of a rumbling noise from the compressor compared to other fridges.

Similarly, there’s Smart Mode, which makes it work more like a thermostat when the fridge is sitting in a warmer temperature. There’s also Party Mode, which prioritizes keeping the drinks cold more so than making less noise. After a few minutes, I did hear the compressor get a little louder. I opened it a few minutes later, and it was definitely colder in there. (Rocco gives the temperature range as 37 to 64 degrees Fahrenheit.)

But if I want the drinks to stay colder while I’m having a party where people are opening it often, I could just lower the temperature to where I want it myself. I really don’t see much of a need for all of these modes. Using a wireless Bluetooth thermometer, I tested the temperature changes inside the fridge for each mode to make sure they work properly. I gave each of them 10 minutes to change and tested each shelf on both ends of the fridge. I was pleased to find these were all within just a few degrees difference of what the fridge read.

The other primary feature of the app is the vision system. When you first set up the app, sensors in the fridge scan everything you’re storing in it. Every beverage then shows up on your app, organized by drawer. I’m storing some pretty obscure drinks, like OoMee algae-infused beverage and Yaté yerba mate, and it recognized most of them, so I was impressed, although some, like my Dolin vermouth, which is one of the most popular vermouth brands, were not recognized.

Nutrition facts also pop up for each drink, although many of them are incomplete. In theory, you could go to the grocery store and see which drinks you’re running low on just by looking at the app. I found that I didn’t do this much, although I was curious if I was running low on LaCroix once and checked the app to see that I certainly was. So it came in handy.

However, the system is not perfect. Right now it’s showing that I still have one LaCroix remaining, although I haven’t had one in there in a couple of weeks. I would love it if I could purchase something I’m running low on directly from the app.

The dual-temperature system also allows you to make half of the fridge one temperature and the other half another, which you can adjust manually or through the app. While this is important so that I can keep seltzers and wines at different temperatures, this is the one feature that’s on many wine fridges, so it’s not unique to the Classic.

The Classic has a kind of mid-century vibe but also feels contemporary. I love the fluted glass door, which looks stunning when it’s nighttime and the lights inside are peeking through it. Any time someone comes to my apartment it becomes a topic of conversation. You can turn the light on and off and adjust the brightness from the app.

The top surface of the fridge is flat and sturdy, so it doubles as a bar cart. The raised lip on the sides also helps so that bottles I’m placing on it have less of a chance of falling off. I have a bar cart that’s overflowing with bottles, so it’s nice to have this right next to it for some overflow.

As someone who loves to make a nightly martini, I’ve hated having to go to my kitchen fridge for the vermouth. Now I store my vermouth right in my Rocco and I don’t have to break up my rhythm as much (other than grabbing ice and the chilled glass from the kitchen freezer). The Classic also comes with a pack of round playing cards that double as coasters. They’re a little flimsy for coasters, but it’s a cute touch.

The fridge beeps when the door doesn’t shut all the way. It’s a pretty soft beep—I didn’t hear it over the TV playing. I wish I got a push notification when the door wasn’t shut. That would have been a much better use of the app. You really have to make sure the door is all the way shut, because it’s not soft-close, nor are the drawers, which I wish were. The small bottom drawer on mine is also a little bit stubborn to pull out and close, although all the other doors slide nice and smoothly.

The price does make your heart skip a beat. But that aligns with other higher-end wine fridges on the market. You also don't need to worry about installing this fridge into your cabinetry, as it’s a stand-alone piece. The precision and engineering of this fridge make the price seem reasonable when compared with others, and it actually has character, whereas just about every other wine fridge looks the same.

Additionally, the price includes a 10-year warranty. For an additional fee, you can get white glove delivery, where it’s placed in your home exactly where you want it and the packaging is removed for you. This is probably not worth it. Otherwise, shipping is free.

The Rocco makes your living room more of an active social space by keeping your guests in the same cozy area. It’s furniture, which I wouldn’t say about most other fridges. I think people are going to buy this fridge more because of the way it looks rather than the fact that it’s a smart fridge. I’m a beverage enthusiast, so I love having the Rocco to show for it.

If you're more of a visual person and want a dating experience to match, Cams.com is a great alternative dating platform. As with AFF, the experience is quite restrictive for free members, though it does allow you to browse webcam feeds. The real fun begins when you sign up for an upgraded paid account. You can then access HD webcam feeds, with options to tip, private message, or live video chat with other users.

It also offers a very robust search filter, with models of all legal ages, genders (trans-inclusive!), and ethnicities. One big caveat, though: as with AFF, there are scammers on Cams.com, often using pre-recorded video feeds, so it's always worth taking a second to verify that the person you're watching is real before you spend a token on them or send a DM.

#395. Google Wanted Spirit Airlines Data. Flight Attendants Found a Way to Opt Out

An agreement reached this week between Google and a union representing an unlikely workforce—flight attendants—could reveal a more permanent answer by creating a process that might reliably separate the data that workers produce from their own personal information. A judge still needs to approve the agreement next week.

The revised deal requires Spirit to hire a third-party data de-identification company, called Tonic AI, to exclude information that could potentially be associated with individual consumers or employees. Tonic will also be charged with ensuring that data, once de-identified, cannot be relinked to specific people. Google has promised to maintain the data in this new, de-identified form.

Many sensitive records will be excluded from the sale, including employee medical records, documents related to employee investigations and labor relations, and information about industry-wide safety management systems. In early November, a trade organization representing airlines chimed in on the sale, arguing that including that information could make employees less willing to come forward to report safety issues through voluntary programs, which are widely regarded as critical to the US aviation industry’s strong safety record.

The proposed agreement also includes an opt-out clause. Google can choose to renege on the sale if the data-cleaning process reduces the assets by more than 8 percent. Google didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Association for Flight Attendants president Sara Nelson tells WIRED she’s as surprised as anyone that flight attendants are at the forefront of AI-related workers’ rights issues, which often focus on employees who, willingly or unwillingly, train their machine replacements.

“It’s very hard to replace a flight attendant—you’d need a high-functioning robot, and that seems to be further off,” she says. “What this shows is that this is an issue even in jobs you think are most protected from AI. This is an issue for everyone.”

She said the union will immediately begin to demand that other airlines include worker-data-protection clauses in their labor agreements. “If you’re not willing to meet these standards for your workers, we’re going to shame you,” she says. The Association for Flight Attendants has begun meeting with state-level politicians to craft legislation that would write worker data protections into law.

Tech leaders have argued that workers understand that their information will train AI models, which will ultimately make their lives better and easier. “You have to think of the upside, the abundance that AI can result in,” one executive told WIRED this month.

Nelson says US workers aren’t buying the upside of AI and that they’re part of the wider electorate that seems to be growing warier of the tech by the day. She says the vision of AI abundance is “a fantasyland of people in boardrooms with beanbags who wear hoodies.”

#394. What to know about this year’s UN climate talks

Climate finance and fossil fuels top the formal agenda at COP31.

It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey.

COP31 officially kicked off on November 8, marking the beginning of negotiations on one of the biggest stages of the climate world. Turkey and Australia are cohosting this year’s talks, which are scheduled to wrap up on November 20.

This annual gathering can often serve as an indicator of where the world stands on addressing and adapting to the climate crisis. And this year’s talks are sure to be a doozy—expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance in particular. Here’s what you should know about COP31.

In recent years, the tension always feels high when COP rolls around. (COP stands for “Conference of the Parties.”) But this year feels especially charged: The world is still grappling with the ongoing war in Iran, which has disrupted the Middle East and sent economic shock waves around the world as energy prices have spiked.

This year’s COP will be the second without a formal delegation from the US. President Trump formally withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement earlier this year and is in the process of withdrawing from the UN Framework Committee on Climate Change. That’s the treaty that allows formal participation in negotiations.

Meanwhile, things aren’t looking good for the Paris Agreement, which was established at UN climate talks 11 years ago, setting a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 °C over preindustrial levels. In a report published in September, the UN Environment Program acknowledged that global warming is set to exceed that 1.5 °C goal, “likely within the next few years.”

So as climate talks kick off, there’s an obvious, urgent question looming about how to quickly cut emissions to limit warming. There’s also the major issue of how to pay for efforts to address emissions and to help a warming world endure the inevitable damage.

Two years ago, talks ended in a goal of mobilizing $300 billion per year by 2035 to help pay to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. (Rich nations provided $136.7 billion in 2024, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development.) And last year, the COP30 agreement included a goal of tripling the money for adaptation over that period. (Such funding has been quite flat over the past few years.)

The world got a tragic reminder of just how high the stakes are earlier this year, when a glacier collapse caused devastating flooding in the Himalayas. The flood killed approximately 1,500 people, left over 5,000 missing, and caused nearly $5 billion in damage. The UN loss and damages fund committed $20 million to helping Nepal recover (less than 1% of the total estimated cost to the country).

Another key trend to watch is how the formal negotiations engage with the topic of fossil fuels. Three years ago, the final agreement text explicitly called for a transition away from them. But it felt as if things took a step back last year, when the final agreement didn’t even mention the phrase “fossil fuels” once. This will be an interesting conversation, especially because cohosts Turkey and Australia have both faced criticism over their relationships with these fuels—Australia is a major exporter of coal and natural gas, and Turkey’s grid relies heavily on fossil fuels, including coal.

Outside the formal negotiations, COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister, is spearheading a side agenda, including two informal initiatives that will be worth watching. These wouldn’t be part of the official agreement text, but countries could sign on to signal support.

One is a pledge to make AI more sustainable; this is almost comically squishy, even as voluntary COP pledges go. The text includes explicit wording that it creates no new obligations for countries, so don’t expect anything resembling enforcement there.

The COP leadership is also pushing to make electricity a larger part of member countries’ energy use. Today, only about 23% of global energy is used in the form of electricity. Fossil fuels, like gasoline in vehicles or natural gas for heating, make up the bulk of the rest. Shifting to more electricity use, and relying on cleaner sources for that electricity, could help drive down emissions. The new pledge’s target is for electricity to make up 35% of total energy consumption by 2035.

With leadership billing this as an “implementation COP,” it would be great to see some real, tangible progress on the global challenge of addressing climate change. I’m not expecting anything groundbreaking, but we’ll be tuned in to see what the final agreement shapes up to be.

This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here.

#393. Apple Watch Ultra 4 vs. Ultra 3: Why you might want to upgrade to Apples new rugged smartwatch

Apple dropped a new premium rugged smartwatch this fall, the Apple Watch Ultra 4. While it looks the same as its predecessor on the outside, don't be fooled: Its has some updated internal hardware and fresh features that make it "an essential upgrade" for certain users, according to our reviewer.

Here's a closer look at the key differences between the Apple Watch Ultra 4 and last year's Apple Watch Ultra 3.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Ultra 3 both start at $799 in one size with cellular connectivity. The latter is no longer available in new condition through the Apple Store, but third-party retailers were still selling it as of this writing.

As mentioned up top, both Apple Watch Ultras look virtually identical. They both have 49mm titanium cases that are water-resistant for up to 100 meters. The Ultra 4 is just slightly heavier by up to 1.4 grams, depending on the case color, and the back of it is made from ceramic and zirconia instead of ceramic and sapphire crystal.

Apple didn't make any changes to the Ultra's display between the two generations. The Ultra 3 and 4 both have a wide-angle, always-on OLED display with up to 3,000 nits of brightness. They're 50 percent brighter than the standard Apple Watch Series 12.

The titanium cases on the Ultra 3 and 4 both come in the same two colors: natural and black. You can pair them each with an Alpine Loop, Trail Loop, Ocean Band, Titanium Milanese Loop ($100 extra), or premium bands from the Apple Watch Hermès collection that Apple designed in partnership with the luxury French fashion brand. Those cost a pretty penny.

Apple rolled out several new band colors and one new Hermès band style for the Ultra 4. They also fit the Ultra 3, and you can buy them separately for $99 to $2,199:

Alpine Loops: Desert, dark olive, and burgundy

Trail Loops: Dark umber, sand, and burgundy

Ocean Bands: Translucent gray, translucent kelp, and translucent black

Apple Watch Hermès collection: Grand H Titane band

Like the Series 12, the Ultra 4 runs on Apple's brand-new S11 chip, which makes it capable of taking more accurate step counts and running some new Audio Intelligence tools (more on those shortly). The Ultra 3 has an older S10 chip.

Both Apple Watch Ultras support WiFi 4 and Bluetooth 5.3, and come equipped with 64GB of built-in storage.

The Ultra 3 is a very long-lasting smartwatch, but thanks to that S11 chip, the Ultra 4 can stretch its battery life even further in a bunch of different scenarios. It's rated for up to 50 hours of normal usage and 84 hours in Low Power Mode, which is a boost of up to 19 percent compared to the Ultra 3. It taps out at 42 hours of normal usage and 72 hours in Low Power Mode. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Both Ultras can charge to 80 percent battery in about 45 minutes, but the Ultra 4 charges quicker on shorter cycles. Fifteen minutes on an outlet gives it up to 18 hours of normal use, while a five-minute charge delivers up to 10 hours of sleep tracking. Those numbers dip down to 12 hours and 8 hours, respectively, with the Ultra 3.

The Ultra 4 also has new Extended Workout and Max Extended Workout modes. These get you up to 25 and 45 hours of usage during endurance activities while the watch is taking constant GPS and heart rate readings.

Chip and battery life aside, the Ultra 4's biggest hardware upgrade comes in the form of its new optical and electrical heart sensors. The former glow green on the underside of the device.

Thanks to these sensors, Apple said the Ultra 4 takes more frequent and accurate heart-rate readings and measures heart rate variability (HRV), a marker of stress and recovery, up to 24 times more often than the Ultra 3. You can now compare your daytime and nighttime HRV measurements as well.

Both Ultras run on watchOS 27 and support Apple Intelligence tools like and Siri AI. Key health and safety features like hypertension notifications, sleep apnea alerts, blood oxygen readings, cycle tracking, and Emergency SOS via Satellite are available on either model. But since the Ultra 4 has a more powerful chip and better sensors, it can do a couple things that the Ultra 3 can't.

One is calculate a Readiness score, which tells the user how fit they are for future exercises on a scale of 0 to 10. This score is based on their recent activity, vitals, and quality of sleep.

The Ultra 4 also has a redesigned pedometer model that can track steps more accurately and a new Steps complication on its watch face. On older Apple Watch models, a step count widget is something you have to DIY.

Finally, the Ultra 4 adds Audio Intelligence tools like Sound Recognition alerts, Live Rewind conversation transcriptions, Siri Recap conversation summaries, and automatic music recognition via Shazam, which rely on its built-in microphone. Apple said they don't create or store any audio recordings, and that raw audio is processed separately from the rest of the system before being deleted. But if you're too sketched out by them, you can just turn them off.

All of these new features are also available on the Apple Watch Series 12, which has the same upgraded chip and sensors as the Ultra 4.

After testing the Apple Watch Ultra 4 for a few days prior to its release, Mashable senior editor Stan Schroeder concluded that it's "an essential upgrade" for "an athlete, especially an endurance athlete, who needs the best battery life and the best heart rate measurement system available." If your workouts aren't quite as intense, you'll probably be content with an Ultra 3.

It should be noted that the Ultra 3 is easier to find on sale these days since it's an older device. (It's been as cheap as $649 a couple times and regularly falls to $699, while the Ultra 4 has only hit $699.99 once so far since launch.) If you want a fancy and durable wearable at a great value, monitor retailers' listings for deals in the coming weeks, especially around Black Friday. That said, if both models are sitting at their usual price of $799 when you go to buy one, you might as well get the nicer Ultra 4.

#391. Alex Karp Said He’s a ‘Progressive.’ OK! Here’s Some Other Stuff He’s Said Recently

When Palantir chief executive Alex Karp sat down with Politico this week, he reportedly used the word “progressive” eight times to describe both his political philosophy and his company.

“I’ve been a Democrat my whole life,” Karp told Politico, which noted that he called the Democratic Party “totally irresponsible” in the distant time of October 2025. “I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir—all of our products are essentially progressive.”

This isn’t the first time Karp has called himself a progressive. In 2018, The New York Times reported that Karp described himself as such. In the same article, he claimed to have voted for Hillary Clinton.

Karp has also donated money to Democratic candidates. In 2023, for instance, he donated $360,000 to a joint fundraising committee for Joe Biden and Kamala Harris. The next year, he donated $1 million to MAGA, Inc.

Palantir has a share of supporters from the Democratic party. However, it’s not necessarily clear how the products of Palantir—a company that built the technology that underpins much of the Trump administration's brutal arrest and deportation campaign, sold tools to the US military that can use generative AI to help plan and execute drone strikes, and partnered with the Israeli military to assist in its devastating war on the Gaza strip, among other things—could reasonably be seen as progressive.

It’s instructive, then, to look at what else Karp has said in recent weeks, and how it lines up with his idea of what’s “progressive.”

In his most recent quarterly letter to Palantir shareholders, Karp actually doubled down on his basic premise. In it, he argued that Palantir employees are “the pioneers of a genuine and viable antiwar movement.”

“We are all, in no uncertain terms, living through what John Lewis Gaddis, the professor of naval and military history at Yale, presciently described decades ago as the long peace,” Karp wrote, despite the fact that the US and Iran are currently engaged in direct warfare.

During Palantir’s corresponding earnings call on November 2, Karp was asked to clarify the statements in his letter.

“Our products are built to avoid war, meaning the adversary knows that they will have such pain inflicted upon them that in fact it's not worth going to war,” Karp said. He did not, however, address the relevant possibility that the US is the party that initiates war.

“I grew up as a lefty,” Karp continued. “I don't actually like war. I want to avoid war. I don't support wars.” But he said, “Sometimes they are necessary, and when they are necessary, America and its allies need the very, very, very best tools.”

Karp went on to say that Palantir has both a “moral imperative” and a “mission reason” for having the “somewhat crazy aspiration” of dominating its market. That mission, Karp said, is supporting the war fighter. Conveniently, it’s also very profitable.

“We are delighted that we can support the war fighter even more because we're making so much money,” Karp said.

Karp’s recent comments in Politico could also be seen through the lens of convenience. Democrats will have a majority in both chambers of Congress next year, and since about half of Palantir’s revenue comes from government work, it’s pragmatic to sow goodwill. Palantir has seen continued success, after all, across Democratic and Republican administrations.

However, Karp doesn’t care about cultivating favor with everybody. He pointedly excludes anyone who has criticized Palantir in what he calls “ridiculously stupid and malicious, incredibly hard to understand attacks.” (Karp didn’t name examples, although many critiques of Palantir have come from the American left.)

“What motivates me is helping to make sure we are fighting for you,” Karp said, addressing Palantir investors, “and quite frankly, making sure that the people that made fun of you and made fun of us are suffering.”

#390. Apple iPhone Duo, one month in: Im never going back to the Pro

Apple's iPhone Duo has been my main phone for a month. I switched from the iPhone 17 Pro Max (I only tested the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max for a week), set up all my apps (including online banking and other finance apps, which typically require a more complicated setup) on the Duo, and put my other phones in a drawer.

This is a different type of test than a typical phone review. When you're writing a review, you're looking for the new and exciting. Once you've switched to a new phone entirely, you're looking for apps that don't work and annoyances that can't be fixed. Had I found enough of these, I would've gone back to the Pro.

But I feel zero desire to do so. The iPhone Duo has plenty of quirks, but none that would make me go back. In fact, I dread the moment when I'll have to go back to a regular-sized phone to do a review. The iPhone Duo is a game-changer for me. I am now a foldable phone guy.

For my detailed review of the iPhone Duo, go here. In this article, I'll skip the details and highlight the interesting bits.

My iPhone Duo works just as well as it did on the first day. I know that some unlucky folks have had screen trouble, but I haven't had anything of the sort so far. The dreaded crease is still barely visible. The hinge works smoothly. In fact, the only real trouble I've had with the Duo has been grease buildup on the inner display, which appears near-impossible to remove (but is, fortunately, invisible most of the time).

Not only did the hardware hold up, but I've gotten completely used to it. I perform the little tasks (check out a message, see the weather forecast) on the front display; I flip the phone open for anything taking longer than five seconds. It's become second nature, and I don't think about it anymore. I still awkwardly search for the volume buttons sometimes, but even that doesn't bother me much; I know they're there, somewhere.

The camera is the Duo's weak point, and I do miss the telephoto option. If there's one thing that would make me go back to a non-Duo phone, it would be the camera. The Duo's camera isn't bad, but it's roughly in line with what you'd get on an iPhone 16 or 17, and that can be hard if you've used a recent Pro model. For now, I'm sticking with it, but I really hope the next Duo gets a lot of improvements in this area.

Battery life isn't a problem. It's not as good as battery life on the iPhone 18 Pro Max, but it the Duo lasts a full day for me. It really depends on how you use it, and the Duo beckons you to use it more for gaming and videos, which drains the battery faster. Still, I've never had to charge it more than once per day, which is good enough for me. The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

By far the most annoying bugs have to do with the fact that the iPhone Duo has four cameras and many apps still don't know when to invoke which one. Making a video call on Messenger, WhatsApp, or Apple's own FaceTime will yield different results depending on how the phone is turned; sometimes you'll be upside down for no good reason. Sometimes, the person you're on a call with will be in a narrow, vertical window awkwardly positioned in the middle of that large, horizontal inner display. I have no doubt this will all get fixed over time, but it is taking a bit too long.

The other annoyance is that some apps still haven't been properly updated for the Duo, and that could take months or perhaps years to fix. This includes some apps I use daily, such as Google Authenticator and TradingView. Others have been tweaked to fit the big display better, but those tweaks were just quick fixes. This isn't hard to get used to, but it just feels like the overall app experience on the Duo could and should be so much better.

The other day, I watched two entire episodes of Slow Horses on the iPhone Duo. I've never done something like that on any phone; the displays were always too small. Given the Duo's screen size, brightness, and quality, watching on the Duo would actually be an improvement over a crappy hotel TV (and TVs in hotels are still very often very crappy).

On my desk, I now have the iPhone Duo all the time as an additional display. I use it to control music, check my calendar and reminders, and manage my smart home devices. In fact, wherever I go, I prop the Duo up beside me; it's like a more portable HomeView.

Showing a bunch of photos to someone, playing a video for a group, and browsing through a shopping site together with my wife are all tasks that are borderline annoying on a regular phone, and almost invariably end with someone giving up very quickly. On the Duo, the experience is great, and is invariably greeted with the same comment: "That screen is nice."

Oh, and the fact that the stereo speakers are pretty great also helps a lot when you're playing music on the Duo. Theoretically, you can prop up any phone on a table and play music, but you'll rarely do it because the sound is thin and tinny. On the Duo, it's good enough to be the background entertainer at a small gathering.

Keeping it simple: How many times do I hold the Duo in my hand and think, "damn, I wish I had a different phone now"? The answer is never. Or, perhaps, only when I need to take a photo, and even then the Duo is better for actually viewing the photos I've taken.

The advantages of having an iPhone with a massive, beautiful, iPad mini-like display in your pocket simply outweigh all of the compromises that you have to make with the Duo. And I don't see myself going back anytime soon.

Stan is a Senior Editor at Mashable, where he has worked since 2007. He's got more battery-powered gadgets and band t-shirts than you. He writes about the next groundbreaking thing. Typically, this is a phone, a coin, or a car. His ultimate goal is to know something about everything.

#388. Whats new to streaming this week? (Nov. 13, 2026)

Don't be overwhelmed or waste an hour scrolling through your services to determine what to watch. We've got your back, whatever your mood. Mashable offers watch guides for all of the above, broken down by genre: comedy, thriller, horror, documentary, and animation, among others. But if you're seeking something brand new (or just new to streaming), we've got you covered there, too.

What if dinosaurs terrorized a suburb? That's the premise of the latest from writer/director David Robert Mitchell (It Follows). And while there's plenty of action and jump scares in this Amblin-inspired adventure, I was not a fan of The End of Oak Street.

Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor star as an oft-bickering married couple who need to reunite as a team to keep their teenage children from being eaten by the prehistoric creatures prowling their neighborhood. Grim and gory with a dunderheaded ending, I'm not remotely recommending this movie. But it sure is streaming this weekend. — Kristy Puchko, Entertainment Editor

Starring: Anne Hathaway, Ewan McGregor, Maisy Stella, and Christian Convery

How to watch: The End of Oak Street will debut on HBO Max on Nov. 13.

Is this a safe space to admit I've seen every episode of Deadly Women at least once? I won't deny the Investigation Discovery doc series, which ran for over 190 episodes across 14 seasons, is problematic. The show's experts (and writers) tended to frame its subjects under misogynistic archetypes, like deadly gold diggers, ungrateful daughters, and sex-crazed maniacs, with little more than lip service to motives or the societal conditions or psychological distress that led to murder. But I couldn't get enough of the succinct storytelling, which traversed the globe and centuries, to tell stories of all kinds of women who were admittedly deadly.

Deadly Women 2.0 offers a new cast of expert psychologists, along with re-enactments, evidentiary footage, and disturbing new stories. Will this one be better — or less problematic — than its older sister series? I'll definitely be watching to find out. — K.P.

How to watch: Deadly Women 2.0 premieres Tuesday, November 10 at 9 p.m. ET/PT, with new episodes airing weekly. Episodes will be available to stream on HBO Max.

This docu-series traces the origins of looksmaxxing, which is part of the bizarro maxxing trend that Dictionary.com named word of the year. Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death follows the story of Anthony Hughes (aka Tony Huge/Dr. Huge), a fitness influencer and self-described "millionaire lawyer and body-building nerd" whose close friend — and fellow looksmaxxing influencer — Leo Longevity was found dead in Thailand in 2023. "A lot of people in my past have died," Hughes is heard saying in the trailer. "And it's nothing to do with me." — Sam Haysom, General Assignment Editor, UK

How to watch: Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death is now streaming on Hulu.

If you like your found footage horror with a side of grief and misery, you may want to check out Tinsman Road. Writer/director Robbie Banfitch also stars in this story about a man on the trail of his missing sister, who vanished while out walking in the woods around their home long ago. Banfitch's own mother plays his mother in the film, with the two of them battling both their grief and the possibility of something supernatural. This sounds like one for fans of Lake Mungo. — S.H.

Starring: Robbie Banfitch, Leslie Ann Banfitch, Salem Belladonna, and Heather Middleton

How to watch: Tinsman Road debuts on Shudder on Nov. 13.

Karin Slaughter's best-selling thriller The Good Daughter gets the TV treatment this week, with Oscar nominee Rose Byrne and Emmy nominee Meghann Fahy at the helm. The pair play sisters Samantha and Charlotte Quinn, who have spent the past 20 years processing a violent attack on their family. When another act of violence shatters their small town, it dredges up complicated memories and painful family truths. If you love thrillers and all-star casts, The Good Daughter might be right up your alley. — Belen Edwards, Entertainment Reporter

Starring: Rose Byrne, Meghann Fahy, Brendan Gleeson, Harper Steele, Paula Malcomson, Jake McDorman, Olivia Williams, Michael Dorman, Jayson Warner Smith, Audrey Grace Marshall, and Drew Cheek

How to watch: The Good Daughter is now streaming on Peacock.

Portrait photography great Richard Avedon is on the other side of the lens in this Netflix documentary from Ron Howard. Through archival footage and interviews with his family, friends, and contemporaries (Avedon himself passed away in 2004 at the age of 81), the film explores the artist who disrupted and defined modern portraiture.

You would have seen at least one of his signature striking photographs — everyone from Martin Luther King Jr. to Charlie Chaplin, Marilyn Monroe, Michael Jordan, James Baldwin, Andy Warhol, Louis Armstrong, the Dalai Lama, Toni Morrison, The Beatles, and so many more. An overarching picture of the pioneer, Howard looks into Avedon's influence on the fashion world, while examining his need to capture the people instrumental in global politics. — Shannon Connellan, Senior Editor

How to watch: Avedon is now streaming on Netflix.

Abbott Elementary fans know five-time Emmy nominee Janelle James as the always unfiltered, always hilarious principal Ava. But before her role on Abbott Elementary, she was primarily known as a stand-up comedian. Now, audiences can get better acquainted with James' stand-up work in her debut stand-up special, Janelle James: How Romantic. Over the course of the special, James touches on American politics, dating, and more, making for a fun, candid hour of comedy.  — B.E.

How to watch: Janelle James: How Romantic is now streaming on Netflix.

Remember how Odyssey audiences freaked out over the trailer for Jessica Chastain as Other Mommy? Well, now's your chance to get your spine tingled at home by the latest from Rob Savage (Host, The Boogeyman).

Based on Josh Malerman's New York Times best-selling novel Incidents Around the House, Other Mommy centers on Bela (Arabella Olivia Clark), a 7-year-old girl who is being stalked by an entity she calls "other mommy," which looks like her real mommy (Jessica Chastain). A haunted house narrative that's thrillingly twisted, gruesome, and stupid, Other Mommy might not be for the whole family. But it's some sick fun. — K.P.

Starring: Jessica Chastain, Jay Duplass, Arabella Olivia Clark, Dichen Lachman, Arian Moayed, Sean Kaufman, and Karen Allen

How to watch: Other Mommy is now available for rental or purchase on digital.

Look, by this point, chances are you've already seen Avengers: Endgame. But if you need to rewatch it as part of your preparation for Avengers: Doomsday, be sure to watch Avengers Endgame: Encore, debuting Friday on Disney+. It's the same tale of the Avengers battling fight Thanos (Josh Brolin) and trying to reverse his catastrophic snap, only this time, there are a few extra scenes tacked on at the end that tease what's to come in Doomsday. — B.E.

Starring: Robert Downey Jr., Chris Evans, Mark Ruffalo, Chris Hemsworth, Scarlett Johansson, Jeremy Renner, Don Cheadle, Paul Rudd, Brie Larson, Karen Gillan, Danai Gurira, Benedict Wong, Jon Favreau, Bradley Cooper, Gwyneth Paltrow, and Josh Brolin

How to watch: Avengers Endgame: Encore hits Disney+ Nov. 13.

If you love your TV shows full of flashbacks and non-linear storytelling, do I have a show for you! Feast your eyes on 12 12 12, which follows a heist across three different timelines: the 12 months of planning leading up to it, the 12 hours of the heist itself, and the 12 days following the heist. Jamie Dornan plays longtime thief Paul Galvin, and Anthony Mackie plays FBI agent Jack Strickland, who's diligently on his tail. Together, the pair face off in a cat-and-mouse game that may sneakily get you in the holiday spirit, as the heist takes place on Christmas Eve. — B.E.

Starring: Anthony Mackie, Jamie Dornan, Jack Kesy, Kali Reis, Ólafur Darri Ólafsson, Agathe Rousselle, Sallie Harmsen, and Patrick Fabian

How to watch: 12 12 12 debuts on Apple TV on Nov. 13.

A Charlie Brown Christmas is a holiday classic, and this week, Apple TV hopes to add another Peanuts special to your winter rotation.

In Snoopy Presents: 12 Days of Snoopy, Charlie Brown's beloved beagle has wound up on Santa Claus's naughty list. Now, with only 12 days left until Christmas, he'll have to prove he's a good dog, and of course, learn some valuable holiday lessons along the way. Get ready for some Christmas sweetness, as well as jazzy music from composer Jeff Morrow and original music from John Legend, Kamasi Washington, Leon Bridges, and Laufey. — B.E.

Starring: John Legend, Kamasi Washington, Leon Bridges, and Laufey

How to watch: Snoopy Presents: 12 Days of Snoopy debuts on Apple TV on Nov. 13.

From Siân Heder, the director behind the Best Picture Oscar winner CODA, comes Being Heumann, a biographical drama about Judith Heumann, an advocate known as the mother of the disability rights movement.

An adaptation of her memoir Being Heumann: An Unrepentant Memoir of a Disability Rights Activist, this movie focuses on the 1977 sit-in that began as an impulsive political action and became the longest occupation of a federal building in American history. Sounds like a stirring drama that could well return Heder to the Oscar campaign trail. While critics have cheered the film's performances, from a compelling cast of actors with disabilities, they've been less impressed with Heder's filmmaking. Essentially, this is a movie about revolution that feels frustratingly traditional.* — K.P.

Starring: Ruth Madeley, Mark Ruffalo, Dylan O'Brien, Rob Delaney, and Ray Fisher

How to watch: Being Heumann debuts on Apple TV on Nov. 13.

Jessica Chastain's country-music-filled thriller comes to Netflix this week, from writer/director Shana Feste (Country Strong). Heartland sees Chastain playing Misty Jones, a country music star who has stepped out of the spotlight — and, unfortunately, into the role of amateur investigator. Returning to her hometown of Nashville 20 years later, she's tracking the disappearance of her 22-year-old niece, Charlie Heart (Carter Faith), a rising country star. Decades since she's been in town, Misty must determine suspects from allies in the city that made her. — S.C.

Starring: Jessica Chastain, Garrett Hedlund, Carter Faith, and John Hawkes

How to watch: Heartland debuts on Netflix on Nov. 13.

Imagine if 20 years after the events of E.T., Elliott hadn't moved on from obsessing over his alien friend. That's essentially the premise of the oddball Aussie comedy Allen.

When Petey (T.J. Power) was a kid, he met a cute extraterrestrial he named Allen. But after playing together and making a pact to be besties for all time, Allen took off to parts unknown. Decades later, Petey hasn't grown up, rejecting building a career, a relationship, or a family while he waits for Allen to return. But when he does, their reunion sparks a bizarre revelation that will force Petey and his human loved ones to come together to save the world.

From Daley Pearson, co-founder of Bluey production company Ludo Studios, Allen offers a family-friendly setup with comedy that's decidedly not! But for those who grew up on the '80s, there's plenty of irreverent humor, heart, and nostalgia to enjoy. — K.P.

Starring: T.J. Power, Charlotte Nicdao, Josh Helman, Emily Barclay, and Benedict Hardie

How to watch: Allen is now streaming on Netflix.

The Proud family is back, but with a Rankin/Bass twist! Leaning into the classic aesthetic of the animators who brought us stop-motion classics like Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer and Santa Claus is Comin' to Town, A Proud Family Wizmas reimagines its 2D clan in a new dimension.

When businessman Wizard Kelly rebrands Christmas as Wizmas, Penny Proud sounds off at a mall Santa, hurting the holiday spirit. Now, it's up to her to Santa Clause it up and save Christmas. We're always game for more Proud family fun. So, the holiday flare plus the stop-motion reimagining is the cherry on top of our whipped cream and hot cocoa. — K.P.

Starring: Kyla Pratt, Tommy Davidson, Paula Jai Parker, Jo Marie Payton, Cedric the Entertainer, Karen Malina White, Soleil Moon Frye, Alisa Reyes, Carlos Mencia, Alvaro Gutierrez, Raquel Lee Bolleau, and Melissa De Sousa

How to watch: A Proud Family Wizmas debuts on Disney+ on Nov. 14.

Rivals enters its darkest days yet, as the lauded Jilly Cooper adaptation returns in uncharacteristically sombre form for Season 2, Part 2. But this is the Cotswolds in the '80s — there's also plenty of drama and debauchery. Reeling from a major character death at the end of Part 1, the residents of Rutshire are grieving, guilt-ridden, and swiftly pivoting to post-funeral sex to the sounds of George Michael’s "Faith." As the feud between Rupert Campbell-Black (Alex Hassell) and Lord Tony Baddingham (David Tennant) reaches a point of no return, secret affairs hide an inch from discovery, unexpected new romances simmer, and the all-important war for commercial television dominance raises the stakes for one of the most superbly salacious shows on TV. — S.C.

Starring: David Tennant, Aidan Turner, Katherine Parkinson, Victoria Smurfit, Alex Hassell, Nafessa Williams, Bella Maclean, Emily Atack, Lisa McGrillis, and Danny Dyer

How to watch: Rivals Season 2, Part 2 debuts on Disney+ on Nov. 11.

All hell breaks loose in Netflix's new series The Body, about a Catholic high school dance team who might have summoned the Devil.

Created by Quinn Shephard (Under the Bridge), The Body is an intoxicating blend of strange visions, sapphic angst, and religious hysteria, led by a formidable young cast. As I wrote in my review, "Mix the teen-girl ferocity of Yellowjackets with the moral panic of The Crucible, dress it up in a blinged-out Juicy Couture tracksuit, and you'll get The Body." Come on, who wouldn't want to give that a whirl? — B.E.

Starring: Kristina Bogic, Sara Boustany, Geena Meszaros, Nnamdi Asomugha, Louisa Krause, Shirley Chen, Jackson Kelly, and Sofia Wylie

How to watch: The Body is now streaming on Netflix.

The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power returns for Season 3, and this time, Sauron (Charlie Vickers) is running the show. He's conquered most of Middle-earth and is working on forging one ring that will force all other rings of power to bend to his will. Can the rebellious Elves, Dwarves, and Men of Middle-earth stop him in time? If you have any passing knowledge of J.R.R. Tolkien's work, you know the answer. But, as is the case with Tolkien, the journey to the end point is where the real fun happens.

While The Rings of Power still struggles with its pacing and unwieldy scale, Season 3 is the show's most fun outing yet. Turns out, it's a total blast watching Sauron be fully evil and corrupt those around him, just as it's a blast to watch the show's spectacular fight sequences. And with the introduction of new characters like Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower), Galadriel's (Morfydd Clark) long-lost husband, there's many a new juicy dynamic to explore. — B.E.

Starring: Morfydd Clark, Charlie Vickers, Robert Aramayo, Ismael Cruz Córdova, Cynthia Addai-Robinson, Charles Edwards, Owain Arthur, Maxim Baldry, Jamie Campbell Bower, Trystan Gravelle, Robert Strange, Markella Kavenagh, Daniel Weyman, Eddie Marsan, Andrew Richardson, Zubin Varla, Adam Young, and Simon Pegg

How to watch: The first four episodes of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 are now streaming on Prime Video, with more every Wednesday.

Philomena Cunk (Diane Morgan) has taught audiences about life and earth in outrageously funny satirical mockumentaries. Now, she's tacking the history of movies with Cunk on Cinema.

Reaching back to the earliest days of the moving image, this mini-series, made up of six 15-minute episodes, offers many actual facts about the evolution of cinema, moving from Edison and Kuleshov to Spielberg and AI. Of course, through the lens of this deadpan and daft character, the results are a mix of informative and chaotically comedic. I warn you, it's hard to watch just one. I binged the whole lot in one sitting, cackling so hard and often that my face hurt in the end. Cheers to Cunk, and all the bewildered interviewees who endured her. — K.P.

Starring: Diane Morgan, Michael Bay, and Benedict Cumberbatch

How to watch: Cunk on Cinema is now streaming on Netflix.
