#386. You Can Buy T-Shirts Glorifying Mass Shootings Almost Anywhere Online

On the day he carried out the Columbine High School massacre, 18-year-old shooter Eric Harris wore a white T-shirt with the phrase “Natural Selection” printed on it in black lettering. His fellow assailant, 17-year-old Dylan Klebold, wore a black T-shirt with the word “Wrath” printed in red across the chest.

Ever since, this apparel has been closely linked with mass murder, part of an ever-growing mosaic of niche allusions to deadly attacks on schools, places of worship, government buildings, and social gathering spaces. While you might not think twice about a person wearing one of the shirts Harris and Klebold chose for their assault on their classmates, let alone recognize the reference, there’s an online community that revels in this aesthetic, using it as a means to valorize and motivate nihilistic violence.

According to a report publishing later this week from the Institute for Strategic Dialogue, a research organization that analyzes extremism and online threats, statement shirts associated with such horrific acts are widely available from at least half a dozen internet retailers.

ISD found sellers peddling “Wrath” and “Natural Selection” tees modeled after the Columbine shirts on TikTok Shop, Redbubble, Temu, Etsy, AliExpress, and Walmart. Shirts with the slogan “Humanity Is Overrated”—like the one worn by a teen gunman who killed nine people at his high school in Finland in 2007—turned up on AliExpress, Temu, and the TikTok Shop, according to the report.

In a statement, a representative for TikTok US said: “Discriminatory and offensive products are prohibited from sale on TikTok Shop and will be removed.” A representative for Redbubble said that the marketplace prohibits “content that glorifies or trivializes violence” and that it had removed listings for “Wrath” and “Natural Selection” shirts flagged by WIRED.

None of the other retailers immediately replied to a request for comment.

Katherine Keneally, ISD’s senior director of threat analysis and prevention, tells WIRED that these clothes are promoted by a cohort known as the True Crime Community, or TCC. Not to be confused with fans of podcasts and documentaries about unsolved or unusual crimes, the TCC “is a predominantly online fandom that is rooted in an obsession with mass killers, regardless of the mass killer’s motivation,” Keneally says.

The TCC’s fascination with the lore around specific killers can lead to dissection of details as minor as what they had for breakfast on the morning of their attack, Keneally says. But the statement shirts offer a convenient way to covertly endorse such massacres, with most people outside the in-group none the wiser.

“What we see from attackers is that they are often trying, in many ways, to mirror previous attackers, but putting their own sort of spin on it,” Keneally says. The shirts are used to “signal interest and glorification of the violence, and also can serve as a sign of someone's plans to engage in something, engage in some sort of attack,” she adds. The ISD’s report cites the cases of a 13-year-old arrested in South Africa last month after allegedly stabbing a 6-year-old while wearing a “Wrath” shirt and an 18-year-old accused of fatally shooting two people in a California library in June, who was apprehended wearing a “Natural Selection” tee.

The ISD analysis of the sale of shirts connected to past shootings is part of a planned series by the nonprofit covering various warning signs of future attacks. The idea is to give parents, teachers, and law enforcement more guidance in understanding when a young person may have intent to harm others, particularly because “within the TCC, we are seeing predominantly youth and minors being involved,” Keneally says.

Adolescents aren’t just engaging with this content in “the darker corners of the internet,” Keneally says. “It's happening very openly across mainstream and fringe platforms.” The prevalence of the clothing across an array of online shops is an indication of how the TCC’s extremist messaging flies under the radar.

Meanwhile, as ISD revealed in its research, younger affiliates of this diffuse collective are trading tips on how to disguise the meaning of paraphernalia tied to mass shooter fandom. One screenshot in the report shows a TikTok user asking their followers, “How do y’all convince your parents to buy the natural selection shirt,” with commenters advising that they pretend “Natural Selection” is the name of a movie, a video game, or a brand. One person replied: “My parents don’t know what tcc is so i can buy it without any problems.”

TCC enthusiasts have also made it clear in their product reviews of the T-shirts that they admire perpetrators of deadly gun violence. In their five-star feedback on a “Wrath” shirt, a customer wrote “we love dylan klebold!” Another attached an anime-style cartoon of Eric Harris in the “Natural Selection” shirt on their review of same, noting that they were hiding it from their mom but that it was “so cute” and “good quality too.” A third person ominously noted that they would use their “Wrath” shirt “to become a bit more popular at school.”

Keneally acknowledges that there’s a “fine line” to consider with clothing that may suggest an unhealthy fixation on infamous killers, since even the best-known examples are not offensive or illegal in themselves. Context also matters: The TCC has an affinity for the German industrial band KMFDM because they were a favorite band of the Columbine shooters, but a fan wearing a KMFDM shirt could have no idea of the connection.

While a teen’s purchase of the most flagrant TCC shirt doesn’t help them commit an attack or necessarily indicate the planning of real-world violence, Keneally says, adults should weigh it against other factors. “If they have access to weapons or maybe another student has heard them talk about committing violence, then it can help serve as a warning sign and provide an opportunity for intervention,” she says. And wearing the shirt at all communicates a likely need for mental health support.

As for the retailers that facilitate the sale of this apparel, Keneally believes that if they adequately enforced their established safety policies, much of it would be taken down. The clothes are something that youths seek out to be “a part of” the True Crime Community and fuel this toxic subculture, she says. “It shouldn't be that easy to access.”

#385. Google Fi adds support for a second 5G network, won't say which one

Fi has always supported T-Mobile, but the new one? Google won’t say.

Google has announced a “super network” upgrade for its Fi cell service. For the past few years, Google Fi has operated exclusively on the T-Mobile network, but now it’s adding support for a second 5G network. Oddly, Google refuses to say which one.

Google’s MVNO (mobile virtual network operator) launched in 2015 as Project Fi with support for both T-Mobile and Sprint service. The service initially only worked on Google’s Nexus phones, which would switch between networks based on signal strength. After T-Mobile absorbed Sprint, Fi switched to being a single-network service in the US while continuing to hop between networks for international travel.

With the super network, Google Fi is again a dual-carrier service stateside. Phones connected to Fi will be able to hop between T-Mobile 5G and a different 5G network to provide the best possible connectivity. Google’s blog post announcing the change conspicuously doesn’t mention either network, saying only that it supports “two of America’s best 5G cellular networks.”

We know one of them is T-Mobile, and the other must be either AT&T or Verizon. When reached for comment, a Google spokesperson declined to name the second network, which is odd. Looking at the Fi coverage map, my best guess for the super network partner is Verizon. The shape of unserved regions is a closer match than AT&T, but carriers do tend to fudge the fine details of these maps.

MVNOs don’t always advertise which network they use, and that information is getting harder to find in FAQs and support pages. Google’s Fi FAQ no longer even confirms T-Mobile as a network partner. Google used to be very upfront about its partnership with T-Mobile, pointing out that, unlike most MVNOs, it gets top prioritization on T-Mobile’s towers. Network information like this is really something consumers should have when shopping for plans—you probably know which carriers work best where you spend your time.

There are a few caveats in the super network rollout beyond the mysterious new partner. Currently, network switching is only supported on the Pixel 9, Pixel 10, and Pixel 11 series. Other devices will get access in 2027. You also won’t be able to enjoy traditional dual-SIM functionality if you want Fi to switch networks. This will only work if you have Fi configured as an eSIM with all non-Fi SIMs disabled.

If you meet those requirements, super network support is rolling out now at no additional cost on Unlimited Premium and Flexible plans.

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#384. Rings of Power star Tyroe Muhafidin talks Theos dark side, Witch-king theories, and that heartbreaking death

Tyroe Muhafidin is ready to embrace his villainous side.

The 20-year-old actor plays Theo in The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power, his first professional role. A young Southlander, Theo has spent the first two seasons of the series caught up in a battle between good and evil that he can barely understand. But in Season 3, Theo hopes to take matters into his own hands, a choice that brings him face to face with Sauron (Charlie Vickers).

Over the course of Season 3's first four episodes, Theo officially joins Sauron's army as a Nazgnagôl, or Ring-servant. Later, in one of the show's heaviest scenes, he kills his former mentor, the elf Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova), at Sauron's command. Between accepting a ring of power and murdering Arondir, Theo's arc has bent entirely toward darkness, especially since the Nazgnagôl will soon become entirely corrupted, turning them into the Nazgûl of The Lord of the Rings.

In a conversation with Mashable, Muhafidin unpacked Theo's turn to the dark side, his final scene with Córdova, and whether Theo may become the Witch-king of Angmar, as the show so heavily implies.

This season, Theo gets up close and personal with Sauron. In the first episode, he and the men of Pelargir head to Mordor for a ring of power. Tell me about how the five years under Númenórean rule have led to this decision from Theo.

In the last five years, I think any of those dwindles of hope that Theo had have now all dissipated. Basically, in the first two seasons, Theo was was very hopeful for a better life, and he really did believe that something good was going to come for his people. Then it just became pain upon pain upon pain, and loss upon loss for him. Five years, especially for a human, is enough time to set in stone for him the idea that those good days weren't ever coming, and if he was ever going to have any life that's different to the one that he's having now, it would be in Barad-dûr.

That fight between the Southlanders for the ring is the most involved combat Theo's been in so far. Walk me through training for that scene and embodying that fight-or-die feeling.

I feel like I've never really done anything where I was the attacker. A lot of the stunty stuff that Theo had done prior was always him running away from something. So I feel like this is the first time, and it's showing that he's grown now, and he can take on battles for himself, full-on, headfirst.

That fight was a bit hectic. It took us a few weeks to choreograph and nail down. Adam [Basil], who's the loveliest guy ever — he's this 6-foot-8 guy, and his name on the call sheet was "Big Farmer" — was absolutely a dream to work with. He's on top of me, and you think that he would be heavy, but he did such a great job at keeping his weight just enough off me that it looked like I was holding all this weight. It was really fun, but it was really grueling to shoot. The conditions in Barad-dûr aren't the most fun. There's fire everywhere and blood everywhere, and it's dark. But I guess that's the exact vibe that Sauron's lair would have!

Speaking of Sauron, I'd love to hear more about working with Charlie Vickers this season and establishing that intriguing dynamic between Theo and Sauron.

Working with Charlie was a dream. He'd always had a particular kind of arm around me since the first season. We were all out in New Zealand by ourselves, and he'd invite me around to play FIFA with him a bunch. It was kind of like an uncle relationship, Uncle Charlie. So we already had this dynamic, and now actually working with him, we could actually build upon that kind of big bro energy.

There's been certain moments that they've shared prior, like the moment where Theo held the sword up and said, "Strength to the Southlands." Halbrand, at the time, recognized that. So, I think Sauron had an eye out for Theo. I think the moment that he stepped into Barad-dûr, her knew there was something about this kid.

I love the whole scene where Sauron uses dark magic to invite Theo to commune with his late father. What's running through Theo's mind in that moment as he learns the truth about his father and his ties to Mordor?

At this point, his mind is racing. It's so filled with everything, it would be hard for him to think rationally at all. He just did a complete fight to the death with six other guys, and now he's having to talk to the Dark Lord and meeting his dad all of a sudden, whom he hasn't known for the last 20 years. It's literally the most insane sequence of events, so at this point he's genuinely the most vulnerable, mentally. His brain is at a point now where it will soak up anything that Sauron says to him, and it has left him easy to manipulate.

Finding out who his dad was is a question that he's asked his entire life, and when he learns, it's disbelief and shock. It's one of those things where you've been wondering for so long, so when you find out, you can't believe that it's true anyway. It's this weird, in-between world of knowing now, but still feeling like he doesn't know. I think Sauron can use that uncertainty in his brain, and with the presence of a ring, it was very easy to say what needed to be said.

I have to talk about the Witch-king in the room, because Sauron tells Theo he has it in him to be a sorcerer and a king. Obviously, a very famous sorcerer king with a ring of power in The Lord of the Rings is the Witch-king of Angmar. Are you able to confirm that Theo is going down that path?

[laughs] You could theorize along those lines, maybe, but I guess you'd have to ask [co-creators] J.D. [Payne] and Patrick [McKay] about that one.

Theo puts on the ring and becomes one of the Ring-servants. When did you learn that this darkness was really going to become a part of his arc?

There was always a presence of it from the first season. With the sword hilt, there was already a connection to the dark side, and there was the scene with Waldreg [Geoff Morrell] at the watchtower trying to get him to join him. There've been temptations throughout, and they were planted carefully, so that when it came to the point that he got offered the ultimate question, he'd already been broken down gradually, and let the darkness in so much that it was easy to say yes.

I'd only found out just just before Season 3 I actually get a ring. In the five years prior to that, I'd been poking at J.D. and Patrick saying, "Will I get a ring? Will I get a ring?"

They always flipped it back on me, asking, "Should Theo get a ring?" And I was like, "I don't know. That's too much pressure!"

I did a little bit of sweet talking all the way through, saying it'd be cool to play a villain. Villain arcs are really cool, and there's some cool depth to them. Theo does have a real great sense of depth and reasoning behind his darkness.

Speaking of the rings, they all look different. Did you get a choice in which one you got to put on?

I think I got the coolest. I remember seeing them all and being like, "I hope that one's mine."

Then when I got my costume for the first time, I got to see which ring was mine, and it was exactly the one I wanted. It was my favorite one out of all of them.

We have to talk about the costume, because the image of the Nazgnagôl armor and mask recalls the Nazgûl in Lord of the Rings, and that has a lot of weight for the series. What was it like, stepping into that for the first time?

I'd done a lot of movement workshops and things like that to try and gauge a sense of the power that the Nazgnagôl would have. I'd done it for a few weeks before any kind of costume fitting, but it wasn't until the day that I had my first costume fitting — there was no armor or crown or anything, it was literally just a bunch of black robes — that I immediately could feel the darkness attached to it. You could get a sense of power, even just in the robes. Then at each costume fitting, they introduced more and more to the costume, and then by the last costume fitting, I'd fully felt the power.

I also requested if I could do some movement workshops in the costume, because it was actually really complicated to move in. The crown is essentially an extension of your head, so any movement of your head will be really exaggerated at the end of the crown. We had to figure out how to walk in a way so our heads weren't bobbing a bunch. There was a sense of trying to move like you're floating, because if we didn't do that, the crown would have just made us look goofy.

What's the secret to moving like the Nazgnagôl?

There's a sense of real strength and power, but also a sense of otherworldliness. The Nazgnagôl live in both the mortal life and the immortal life, so we wanted them to move as if they were in between worlds, and they're coming from one world to another. It was very much about moving with a slight bend at the knees, so every time you're moving, it's more of a glide than a walk. I think once the costume's on, though, it does 80 percent of the work for you. You just automatically feel it.

It's very imposing. We've got to talk about the final scene of episode 4, with Arondir's death. Tell me about filming that final scene with Ismael and finding that last connection?

We shot that scene over two weeks, so we'd shot that specific sequence and the stabbing multiple times without getting any close up. We'd done it wide a bunch of times, and every point up until then, we were really light-hearted. We were having fun on set, and then the day came where we were doing our close-ups, and the air just felt cold, and everyone could feel the sad energy. It was so heavily emotional, like for both of us, it was a real bonding and brotherhood moment. We got a lot closer, because we could open up on our feelings. Feeling so deeply at that time in that moment, it really opened up a big space for us to connect. It was fun though. We had a really great time, and it was a really great group of us on set. It was daunting, but it was very fun. It was a big celebration of Ismael and all the hard work that he's put into this job and how awesome Arondir is. I'm so glad that he got to do all this really cool shit at the end.

What was your reaction to first reading that Theo stabs him?

I knew beforehand. I think initially J.D. and Patrick's plan was to wait for me to just get the script and read it, but Charlotte Brandstrom, the first episode director, just blurted it out to me. I was like, "Oh, I guess that was the whole secret they were trying to keep from me."

So, I knew it was coming, but I didn't know how. I knew at some point if I was going to go to the dark side, there would be a confrontation between them, because obviously they're fighting on opposing ends of the war, and they're both frontmen. Reading it, I just didn't imagine it to be as heartfelt as it was. I always thought that it was going to be a lot colder and a lot quicker. So, reading it and seeing how close he was to really accepting Arondir was really heartbreaking. This is actually such a love-filled scene, and that's why it's so tragic and so heartbreaking, because there is so much love between them, and it just disappears in an instant, which leaves a real hollow feeling at the end of the episode.

There's that moment of compulsion from Sauron that makes Theo stab Arondir. What's he thinking at that moment? Is he reevaluating his choice, or is his humanity too far gone?

Theo is definitely someone who's been a product of who his role models are and who is giving him guidance. This is the moment where his two biggest role models in his life at this point are meeting head to head. For the last few weeks, Theo has been under the influence of Sauron. He has been fed however many ideas in his head about the elves. But then when he sees Arondir's face, all those ideas that Sauron had planted disappear, and he's almost ready to accept the hand that's put out in front of him because he can see the the love in Arondir's eyes. That moment when Sauron arrives is him thinking, "Oh yeah, I remember what I'm supposed to be doing now." It flips back into work mode, or servant mode.

Right now we know the Nazgnagôl as Ring-servants, but we know that the final iteration of them is the Nazgûl, who are totally far gone. Assuming Theo stays on this path, what is an element of that transformation that you're most excited to play?

The cool thing about the Nazgnagôl and the Nazgûl is that they have a completely different living experience to anything else in Middle-earth. They are living in between two worlds, and so you're trying to explore what it looks like to be detaching from the mortal world, becoming more spirit-like, and losing a sense of reality while being completely controlled and manipulated. It'll be really interesting because at this point in time, the Nazgnagôl are still men. They have autonomy over themselves and their decisions and what they can do, whereas it'd be great to see them slowly not be able to do that.

The show has such a massive array of locations to visit. Going forward, what is one of the worlds within Middle-earth that you would like to work in?

I would love, love, love to do work in Númenor. The sets are just so magnificent. Everything around it is so glorious and beautiful, and there's a real community vibe. Any time I've been on the sets with the Númenóreans, they all seem to be getting along real well, whereas I've been hanging out with orcs who most of the time aren't that happy. [laughs]

And who is someone from the ensemble you'd love to work with?

I'd love to do work with more or at least more stuff with Leon [Wadham], who plays Kemen. I really wish we had more to do. I love Leon. When we were shooting Season 3, he was actually living above me, so we were constantly just borrowing stuff off each other all the time and just talking about work or whatever. We only ever had two days on set, and it was the last scene of Season 2 and the first scene of Season 3. But I also just think Kemen is not a nice guy.

Every time he's on screen, I'm angry. I don't even care if Theo's on the dark side. He deserves his vengeance a little.

Yeah, I'd love for Theo to face off against Kemen and give him what he deserves.

The interview above was edited for length and clarity.

#383. The haunting Masters meltdown that changed Rory McIlroy's career

Editor’s Note:  This story was originally published in April 2023.

Slumped on his club, head buried in his arm, Rory McIlroy looked on the verge of tears.

The then-21-year-old had just watched his ball sink into the waters of Rae’s Creek at Augusta National and with it, his dream of winning The Masters, a dream that had looked so tantalizingly close mere hours earlier.

As a four-time major winner and one of the most decorated names in the sport’s history, few players would turn down the chance to swap places with McIlroy heading into Augusta this week.

Yet on Sunday afternoon of April 10, 2011, not a golfer in the world would have wished to be in the Northern Irishman’s shoes.

A fresh-faced, mop-headed McIlroy had touched down in Georgia for the first major of the season with a reputation as the leading light of the next generation of stars.

An excellent 2010 had marked his best season since turning pro three years earlier, highlighted by a first PGA Tour win at the Quail Hollow Championship and a crucial contribution to Team Europe’s triumph at the Ryder Cup.

Yet despite a pair of impressive top-three finishes at the Open and PGA Championship respectively, a disappointing missed cut at The Masters – his first at a major – served as ominous foreshadowing.

McIlroy shot 74 and 77 to fall four strokes short of the cut line at seven-over par, a performance that concerned him enough to take a brief sabbatical from competition.

But one year on in 2011, any lingering Masters demons looked to have been exorcised as McIlroy flew round the Augusta fairways.

Having opened with a bogey-free seven-under 65 – the first time he had ever shot in the 60s at the major – McIlroy pulled ahead from Spanish first round co-leader Alvaro Quirós with a second round 69.

It sent him into the weekend holding a two-shot cushion over Australia’s Jason Day, with Tiger Woods a further stroke behind and back in the hunt for a 15th major after a surging second round 66.

And yet the 21-year-old leader looked perfectly at ease with having a target on his back. Even after a tentative start to the third round, McIlroy rallied with three birdies across the closing six holes to stretch his lead to four strokes heading into Sunday.

The youngster was out on his own ahead of a bunched chasing pack comprising Day, Ángel Cabrera, K.J. Choi and Charl Schwartzel. After 54 holes, McIlroy had shot just three bogeys.

“It’s a great position to be in … I’m finally feeling comfortable on this golf course,” McIlroy told reporters.

“I’m not getting ahead of myself, I know how leads can dwindle away very quickly. I have to go out there, not take anything for granted and go out and play as hard as I’ve played the last three days. If I can do that, hopefully things will go my way.

“We’ll see what happens tomorrow because four shots on this golf course isn’t that much.”

The truth can hurt, and McIlroy was about to prove his assessment of Augusta to be true in the most excruciating way imaginable.

His fourth bogey of the week arrived immediately. Having admitted to expecting some nerves at the first tee, McIlroy sparked a booming opening drive down the fairway, only to miss his putt from five feet.

Three consecutive pars steadied the ship, but Schwartzel had the wind in his sails. A blistering birdie, par, eagle start had seen him draw level at the summit after his third hole.

A subsequent bogey from the South African slowed his charge, as McIlroy clung onto a one-shot lead at the turn from Schwartzel, Cabrera, Choi, and a rampaging Woods, who shot five birdies and an eagle across the front nine to send Augusta into a frenzy.

Despite his dwindling advantage and the raucous Tiger-mania din ahead of him, McIlroy had responded well to another bogey at the 5th hole, draining a brilliant 20-foot putt at the 7th to restore his lead.

The fist pump that followed marked the high-water point of McIlroy’s round, as a sliding start accelerated into full-blown free-fall at the par-four 10th hole.

His tee shot went careening into a tree, ricocheting to settle between the white cabins that separate the main course from the adjacent par-three course. It offered viewers a glimpse at a part of Augusta rarely seen on broadcast, followed by pictures of McIlroy anxiously peering out from behind a tree to track his follow-up shot.

Though his initial escape was successful, yet another collision with a tree and a two-putt on the green saw a stunned McIlroy eventually tap in for a triple bogey. Having led the field one hole and seven shots earlier, he arrived at the 11th tee in seventh.

By the time his tee drive at the 13th plopped into the creek, all thoughts of who might be the recipient of the green jacket had long-since switched away from the anguished youngster. It had taken him seven putts to navigate the previous two greens, as a bogey and a double bogey dropped him to five-under – the score he had held after just 11 holes of the tournament.

Mercifully, the last five holes passed without major incident. A missed putt for birdie from five feet at the final hole summed up McIlroy’s day, though he was given a rousing reception as he left the green.

Mere minutes earlier, the same crowd had erupted as Schwartzel sunk his fourth consecutive birdie to seal his first major title. After starting the day four shots adrift of McIlroy, the South African finished 10 shots ahead of him, and two ahead of second-placed Australian duo Jason Day and Adam Scott.

McIlroy’s eight-over 80 marked the highest score of the round. Having headlined the leaderboard for most of the week, he finished tied-15th.

Tears would flow during a phone call with his parents the following morning, but at his press conference, McIlroy was upbeat.

“I’m very disappointed at the minute, and I’m sure I will be for the next few days, but I’ll get over it,” he said.

“I was leading this golf tournament with nine holes to go, and I just unraveled … It’s a Sunday at a major, what it can do.

“This is my first experience at it, and hopefully the next time I’m in this position I’ll be able to handle it a little better. I didn’t handle it particularly well today obviously, but it was a character-building day … I’ll come out stronger for it.”

Once again, McIlroy would be proven right.

Just eight weeks later in June, McIlroy rampaged to an eight-shot victory at the US Open. Records tumbled in his wake at Congressional, as he shot a tournament record 16-under 268 to become the youngest major winner since Tiger Woods at The Masters in 1997.

The historic victory kickstarted a golden era for McIlroy. After coasting to another eight-shot win at the PGA Championship in 2012, McIlroy became only the third golfer since 1934 to win three majors by the age of 25 with triumph at the 2014 Open Championship.

Before the year was out, he would add his fourth major title with another PGA Championship win.

And much of it was owed to that fateful afternoon at Augusta. In an interview with the BBC in 2015, McIlroy dubbed it “the most important day” of his career.

“If I had not had the whole unravelling, if I had just made a couple of bogeys coming down the stretch and lost by one, I would not have learned as much.

“Luckily, it did not take me long to get into a position like that again when I was leading a major and I was able to get over the line quite comfortably. It was a huge learning curve for me and I needed it, and thankfully I have been able to move on to bigger and better things.

“Looking back on what happened in 2011, it doesn’t seem as bad when you have four majors on your mantelpiece.”

McIlroy’s contentment came with a caveat: it would be “unthinkable” if he did not win The Masters in his career.

Yet as he prepares for his 15th appearance at Augusta National this week, a green jacket remains an elusive missing item from his wardrobe.

Despite seven top-10 finishes in his past 10 Masters outings, the trophy remains the only thing separating McIlroy from joining the ranks of golf immortals to have completed golf’s career grand slam of all four majors in the modern era: Gene Sarazen, Ben Hogan, Gary Player, Jack Nicklaus, and Tiger Woods.

A runner-up finish to Scottie Scheffler last year marked McIlroy’s best finish at Augusta, yet arguably 2011 remains the closest he has ever been to victory. A slow start in 2022 meant McIlroy had begun Sunday’s deciding round 10 shots adrift of the American, who teed off for his final hole with a five-shot lead despite McIlroy’s brilliant 64 finish.

At 33 years old, time is still on his side. Though 2022 extended his major drought to eight years, it featured arguably his best golf since that golden season in 2014.

And as McIlroy knows better than most, things can change quickly at Augusta National.

#382. Voyager 1 is about to hit one light-day away. NASAs planning to party.

If you step outside tonight and flick a flashlight toward deep space, that split-second pulse will race through the void at 186,000 miles per second.

The light will continue its journey while you sleep, while you eat, while you go to work. Only when you reach the same time tomorrow could its photons potentially wash over a spacecraft more than 16 billion miles away.

That robotic probe is NASA's Voyager 1, the farthest human-made object in the universe. It will cross the one light-day-away milestone at 5:16 a.m. ET on Wednesday, Nov. 18. One light-day is the distance light travels over 24 hours. Radio signals move at the speed of light, so any message from Earth would need a full day to reach the spacecraft. Considering Voyager 1 never stops moving, that communication lag will only increase.

To mark the occasion, the U.S. space agency has a couple of things planned, one of which involves pointing that flashlight toward the sky. The day after the milestone, you can watch the mission team talk about where the spacecraft has been and how it keeps going.

Voyager 1 left Earth in 1977 to explore the giant outer planets. NASA timed the launch to catch a lineup of those planets that comes around only once every 176 years. The probe finished its tour decades ago but kept going at nearly 38,000 mph. In 2012, it left the heliosphere, the protective bubble the sun blows around our solar system, and entered interstellar space.

Its twin, Voyager 2, took a different path past Uranus and Neptune and left the solar system in 2018. But Voyager 2 won't reach a light-day until November 2035, most likely after it has depleted its fuel.

That's the bittersweet reality of Voyager 1's historic achievement: Both probes are dying, nearly tapped out of their nuclear power sources that turn heat from decaying plutonium into electricity. Since 2024, the team has shut off two science instruments on each spacecraft to stretch what's left. Sooner or later, the power will run out, and no one will be able to talk with the twins at all, regardless of time delays.

For now, though, the mission team is only thinking happy thoughts. The first way to get involved comes after sunset on Tuesday, Nov. 17. NASA is asking people around the world to point a light at the sky to spell out VGR, Voyager's call sign, in Morse code. Morse code is an old telegraph language that turns each letter into a pattern of short and long signals.

The easiest way to do this is with a phone or tablet. NASA built an online flasher that blinks the code for you. After sunset, open the flasher in your device's web browser, point the device's screen at the sky, and let it send the signal. (You can bookmark this story to keep the flasher link handy.)

If you'd rather tap it out yourself, grab a flashlight, and switch it on and off or use your hand to block and unblock the beam. Short flashes, called dots, should last less than a second. Long flashes, called dashes, should last about one second.

You can repeat the pattern as many times as you like.

Now, even if you were to point your flashlight in precisely the direction of Voyager 1, the beam would fan out into a cone billions of miles wide, scattering its photons across the void. Because the light is diluted in space, virtually every photon would sail past the tiny 12-foot spacecraft without ever hitting it.

But it's a symbolic gesture for wishing the old mission godspeed. You can tag @NASA on your photos and videos if you post them to X, Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, or other social media.

The second way to join in the celebration comes at noon ET / 9 a.m. PT on Thursday, Nov. 19. Mission leaders and top NASA science officials will meet at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California to talk about the twins. They'll explain how the spacecraft are holding up, what they're still learning beyond the sun's bubble, and how engineers keep such old hardware running from far away. The public can watch on NASA's streaming service, NASA+, or Youtube.

The team has plenty to talk about. This year, engineers tried a fix they nicknamed the "Big Bang." They turned off three power-hungry devices on each probe that help keep it warm, and at the same time they switched on three lower-power replacements. The swap should keep them running for at least another year.

But at this stage, the team has come to expect the unexpected. Last month, Voyager 1 had a mysterious issue with its thrusters that briefly caused a communication blackout. Engineers are still trying to figure out what caused the problem.

If the distant spacecraft could send you a Morse code message back, perhaps it would say the one recorded on its Golden Record: "ad astera per aspera." In Latin, that means "to the stars through struggles."

#380. Early Black Friday laptop deals are trickling in. Heres what I would buy already.

Black Friday has always been the best time to buy a laptop, and we expect that to hold true in 2026. While the holiday season's top discounts on MacBooks and Windows PCs may not look as great as usual due to industry-wide price hikes — thanks, RAMageddon — they should still be retailers' most competitive offers of the year.

Black Friday laptop deals aren't plentiful just yet, but some of the initial markdowns I've spotted are worth adding to your cart. Amazon is already offering its usual Black Friday discount on certain variants of the MacBook Air, for instance. And Lenovo has several on-sale laptops marked with a "Black Friday Price Guarantee" badge. (That means they for sure won't get any cheaper through Saturday, Nov. 28, the day after Black Friday.)

Meanwhile, HP has fully kicked off its Black Friday Sale already, and it features discounts of up to $550 on one of the best MacBook alternatives I've tested, the OmniBook Ultra 14. Our sister site, CNET, named it their favorite laptop overall.

Check out my running list of the best early Black Friday laptop deals below.

The Mashable Choice Award-winning M5 MacBook Air boasts "a premium design, great speakers, a bright and sharp display," and incredibly impressive performance, said Mashable Tech Editor Timothy Beck Werth. He called it "a damn near-perfect machine" — so suffice it to say, it's our top MacBook for most people. As of mid-November, Amazon has 1TB variants of both sizes on sale for $250 off, starting from $1,349.99.

Black Friday MacBook Air discounts have historically peaked around $250, so I don't expect these deals to improve down the road.

This model with a powerful Core Ultra 7 251HX chip and RTX 5060 graphics is a whopping 38% off ahead of Black Friday, and Lenovo guarantees that its price won't get any lower through Black Friday.

Black Friday falls on Friday, Nov. 27 this year, but most retailers are starting their holiday sales well before then.

Best Buy will begin its extended Black Friday Doorbusters + Deals event on Thursday, Nov. 19, and it will probably bring us the season's best selection of Windows laptop deals. I also expect Best Buy to start matching Amazon's MacBook Air deals at that point.

Amazon's Black Friday Week sale kicks off the very same day. According to a company blog post, it will feature savings of up to 30% on certain Alienware, Acer, Asus, HP, and Lenovo laptops and gaming PCs.

Walmart is hosting two Black Friday Deals events from Nov. 12 to 15 and Nov. 23 to 29. While I don't think they'll be packed with on-sale laptops, Walmart is usually good at scrounging up some decent gaming laptop deals.

Acer, Asus, and Dell have yet to announce their Black Friday plans, but I'll update this story as soon as they're made public.

Haley Henschel is a Chicago-based Senior Shopping Reporter at Mashable who reviews and finds deals on popular tech, from laptops to gaming consoles and VPNs. #379. What happens to mathematics when AI becomes an oracle?

Mathematician Steven Strogatz discusses his new book, Big Math: The Hidden Codes That Run Our World.

Our modern world runs on math, from social media algorithms, package delivery, and weather prediction to medical imaging and machine learning. The rise of computers helped fuel its dominance, enabling us to work with increasingly large numbers that would otherwise be beyond the capacity of our finite human brains. But with the rise of large language models, AI chatbots, and, soon, quantum computing, so-called “big math” is beginning to outstrip its creators entirely. What that means, and how we might adapt, is the focus of a new book, Big Math: The Hidden Codes That Run Our World, by applied mathematicians Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend.

Strogatz is perhaps best known in his field for his co-authorship of a seminal 1998 paper with Duncan Watts on the collective dynamics of small-world networks. He has also studied chaos theory as applied to physics, the geometry of supercoiled DNA, and the biological collective oscillators, such as swarms of synchronously flashing fireflies and crickets that chirp in unison. In 2005, Strogatz extended his study of synchronicity to the crowds that caused the wobbling of London’s Millennium Bridge.

An award-winning communicator, Strogatz wrote three series of columns on mathematics for The New York Times in 2010, 2012, and 2025 and hosted a podcast for Quanta magazine from 2020–2021. He has written four popular books: Sync (2003), The Calculus of Friendship (2009), The Joy of X (2012), and the New York Times bestseller Infinite Powers (2019).

This time around, Strogatz has found a well-matched co-author in Townsend, a younger colleague recently hired at Cornell who studies numerical analysis and deep learning. As senior faculty, Strogatz was assigned to mentor Townsend, and the two men began regularly lunching together in Risley Hall. Strogatz was intrigued by the popular book potential of Townsend’s course on the top 20 algorithms of the 20th century and suggested co-authorship. That concept slowly morphed into a book about big matrix calculations, and then into what became Big Math.

“There are so many books about pure math, as if computers didn’t exist,” Strogatz told Ars. “Alex and I are both very applied mathematicians. We thought there should be a book on computers and math, especially the class of really big problems with billions of variables or parameters that you just can’t approach in your head. A lot of the math we’ve had for centuries perfectly scales up to this computer moment. What the abacus did for arithmetic, the fangcheng (“rectangular array”) board did for systems of linear equations. It was a matrix you could manipulate with your hand and bamboo sticks. So this externalizing of math outside of our heads into our tools is a 2,000-year-old idea.”

Mathematics now faces its greatest challenge yet in the age of AI, sparking heated debates on the role of human reasoning when the machines are making most of the major breakthroughs. “The mathematician in each of us will always want to know more,” Strogatz and Townsend wrote. “The human being must insist that knowledge serves something larger than itself. That might be the work of our century: letting our power grow without losing our soul. Big Math keeps getting bigger. So must we.”

Ars caught up with Strogatz to learn more.

Ars Technica: Let’s start by defining “big math,” because it’s such a broad umbrella term.

Steven Strogatz: Operationally, big math is “big” relative to human cognitive capacity. So it can be surprisingly small and yet big. We also wanted to expand it to things that people would think of as computational engineering—in the building of the Burj Khalifa, that’d be civil engineering or design architecture. It’s there in medical imaging. It’s in getting us to the Moon. The lunar module was controlled by a tiny computer that only had to think about 20 or 30 variables at a time to steer the LEM down to the Moon’s surface. But it’s not something a person could do in their head.

Big Math is not simply big in the ordinary sense of big numbers. There’s an undercurrent in the book about the importance of linearity and sparsity. When problems are linear, they can be scaled up to immense size, and they stay tractable. If they’re non-linear, you don’t have any hope of dealing with them with pure math. You can do them with computers. But for the people who want rigorous theorems, we’re in terra incognita when we deal with anything that’s non-linear and big.

Small math can be very hard. Historically, we had small math problems with one or two variables, arithmetic, algebra that you learn in high school. Even to this day, a lot of pure math is relatively small. It doesn’t concern itself with enormous numbers of variables simultaneously because it’s totally intractable. Cryptography can be small, but it’s so complicated with its non-linearities and other algebraic difficulties. So big is one way to be difficult, but there are a lot of other ways.

Nowadays, trillions of parameters are typical in the biggest of the large language models. But infinity is not big from this point. Infinity, which you would think of would be the biggest of big math, is not because calculus fits perfectly nicely in a human head. Infinity turns out to be very tractable in a way that a billion is not.

Ars: One of your real-world examples of big math is particularly relevant at the moment: mathematics as it relates to the gerrymandering issue.

Strogatz: It’s an interesting question of, what’s a fair map and what’s a reasonable redistricting? The legal system gives us certain criteria, but they are vague. The districts should not be too snakey-looking, not look like salamanders, for instance. The term in the law is ‘compact.’ They should be reasonably compact. But what does that mean mathematically? The districts are also supposed to be contiguous; you don’t want to have separate islands and call that one district. It’s supposed to respect natural boundaries like rivers or other landscape features. Also, each district is supposed to have roughly the same population.

So how to make maps that respect all of the criteria? It turns out there are a lot of ways to make them. Using past voting information, you can stack the deck. That’s what gerrymandering is all about, trying to redistrict in favor of whatever party is in power. There has been a big debate about whether certain maps violate people’s rights. The principle should be one person, one vote. If you do things that dilute somebody’s power so that their votes are wasted, so to speak, that’s traditionally thought to be unfair or maybe even illegal.

The Supreme Court has heard all kinds of cases, but the court is very resistant to the use of math. I quoted [Chief Justice] John Roberts talking about the efficiency gap as one measure of gerrymandering. He referred to it by its Greek letters and said something like, “The average person on the street is just going to think this is gobbledygook, that this is not a criterion that the law should pay any attention to.”

Nevertheless, Moon Duchin and her colleagues showed this very down-to-earth way of generating a big ensemble of reasonable maps that satisfy all the legal criteria so that you have a baseline, you could do the control experiment. What the math does is give you a principled way of generating maps at random that respect the criteria that the law requires, but otherwise are just a random sample of reasonable maps. How often would a map produce the result that the gerrymander intended? If you can show that it’s an extreme outlier, that’s a measure of something. Does it prove malicious intent? Not really. It does prove it’s not typical.

There was an Alabama voting rights case where Roberts actually voted with the plaintiffs, who said that there was real harm being done to Black voters in Alabama with one of Alabama’s maps. The state was claiming there’s no way we could get a reasonable map to have two districts with Black majority voters. Moon Duchin showed that was wrong. You could generate thousands of maps that would do that. So it just wasn’t true what the state had claimed.

After the book was copyedited and ready to go to press, a Supreme Court decision was made that, in fact, you can partisan gerrymander as much as you want. It doesn’t violate the Voting Rights Act. We wrote a more optimistic story.

Ars: How has math changed over time from a philosophical standpoint?

Strogatz: I think a crisp way to encapsulate it is the role of the computer. For a long time, a computer was a servant to mathematicians and engineers and scientists. It was no more philosophically threatening than a microscope or a telescope. It could extend our senses. It’s a chisel, it’s an anvil, it’s a tool. It helped us do calculations faster; things that would be too hard for people to do at scale you could do on a machine. We had mechanical calculators. They became electronic computers in the 1950s with the invention of the transistor and got much faster to give us today’s supercomputers. We program them; they do exactly what we tell them. So they’re servants.

The first philosophically big change is in the 1950s, when computers start to be used as more than servants; they become scouts. You could send the computer out into unknown, unexplored territory in the mathematical landscape. The clearest example was work by Enrico Fermi and his colleagues (Pasta, Ulam, and Tsingou) that we wrote about in the chapter on simulation. Mary Tsingou was the one who did the calculations in what was traditionally called the Fermi-Pasta-Ulam numerical experiment.

What distinguished it from earlier uses of computers is that Fermi and colleagues had no idea what the answer was going to be. It’s one thing to use a computer to calculate the power released by an atomic bomb blast or to calculate an artillery shell’s trajectory. We didn’t know the exact numerical values, but we knew what was happening. With this experiment, they were trying to simulate a simplified model of how atoms could, in the jargon, thermalize as chemical bonds jiggle. You want to see the decay to entropy. How do systems degenerate to greater and greater disorder if they’re just left to their own devices?

Fermi thought that the non-linear aspect of chemical bonds—meaning if you’d stretch a chemical bond by twice as much, it doesn’t pull back exactly twice as hard, so it’s not strictly proportional—might account for the so-called second law of thermodynamics, the decay to entropy. Pencil and paper math was not up to the job because you couldn’t calculate these non-linear interactions far enough to see the decay into entropy.

So they ran it in the computer, and a shocking thing happened: It didn’t decay. It showed a strange echo. You started all the energy in one of the modes of vibration of this system, and then it started to degenerate. But after a while, 98 percent of the energy came back into the original mode. That was the echo that they called a recurrence phenomenon. It led us to a whole new branch of math that we call soliton theory. It was an early indication that once you walk into the nonlinear jungle, human intuition breaks down. We couldn’t walk there, but we sent our scout, this computer probe, into the wilderness of the mind, and it was the only thing capable of doing the calculations and reporting back to us what it found.

Ars: The rapid rise of AI in mathematics has alarmed many in the field, particularly in light of OpenAI’s release last month of 722 AI-generated math papers, dubbed the “mathocalypse.” Technically, AI is also a new tool, but it seems fundamentally different.

Strogatz: So from servant to scout was a new thing, and computing was our partner. At first, it was all very thrilling. It was like having a new Ferrari or something. You could race ahead and then discover things. That’s what Fermi and Ulam said at the time. That was truly amazing. They didn’t know what to expect. The computer was now teaching us by showing us things, but we could still keep up. We could develop these new theories like soliton theory, so we could rationalize what it was showing us.

What’s different now is that it’s going from servant to scout to oracle, where it’s showing us things that we don’t understand and it’s not articulate enough to explain itself. It seems to be right. A clear example would be something like Google Translate, where it’s fantastic at translating one language into another, but it has not discovered new principles of linguistics, or if it has, it can’t tell us what they are.

Likewise, protein folding with AlphaFold that won the Nobel Prize in chemistry a couple of years ago for the people who built it. We now can solve a thousand times more proteins than we had before, but we have not done it by learning new physics or chemistry. It just recognized patterns, but it can’t tell us how it’s doing it. So that’s where we are, and it’s going to get worse.

Ars: In your book, you ask if insight still matters, citing Stephen Wolfram as an example of someone who might answer that question in the negative.

Strogatz: Wolfram’s position is tricky. He pushes computational irreducibility. I love these two words, perspicuous and perspicacious. Systems can be perspicuous; you can see into them. Science has, for thousands of years, concerned itself with systems that are perspicuous, meaning you can get insight into them because you’re so perspicacious. But the question from Wolfram would be, have we been the famous drunk that’s looking under the lamppost for his keys because it’s dark everywhere else? You wouldn’t have any hope of finding them except under the lamppost.

So is it that we’ve artificially restricted ourself to systems that are transparent enough that we can develop science that our insight illuminates? I think Wolfram would claim that most of nature is computationally irreducible in the sense that there is no simple insightful theory into what’s going on. The best you can do is just run a simulation and watch what happens, similar to just letting nature unfold and watch what happens in reality.

In the jargon people use nowadays, you shouldn’t expect a compressed description, a simplified model that will account for what you’re seeing. We have seen those. Newton could explain the motion of the planets from a few simple principles and that worked, but that’s, I think in Wolfram’s take, artificially simple. Most of science is not going to end up being like that. We don’t know if Wolfram is really right about that. Wolfram, I think, is demonstrably right that many computer simulations are computationally irreducible, but nature might not be.

Ars: If you can’t see into the models, and they can’t explain what they’re doing, how do you know they’re right?

Strogatz: Let’s stipulate that we don’t understand them, and that they are not at the present able to explain themselves to us. Let’s put a little asterisk next to that part, though, because it could be that they’ll become very good teachers. Or maybe we don’t understand Google Translate or AlphaFold right now, but we will in 10 years. I do believe that there will be systems that are truly opaque because of human limits, that we just won’t be fast enough or smart enough or have enough memory. AIs will show us something that we just won’t be able to understand even with their help. What happens then?

Then I think math starts to be more like science or medicine, or engineering. At the FDA, for a new drug to be approved, it has to be shown to be safe by doing a lot of controlled studies and randomized trials. There’s a whole methodology for opacity that people in medicine have worked out. But the doctors do not require knowledge of the mechanism of action. You don’t have to know how aspirin works. You don’t have to know how electroconvulsive therapy works for people with intractable depression. Even if we don’t understand, we can still live with these technologies or drugs by these methods. You don’t have to have first principles understanding. If the AI is an oracle, you can still check it by seeing how often it is right.

Strogatz: It is a loss. I don’t want to pooh-pooh the severity of the—to use a fancy philosophical word—epistemic loss. What we have prided ourselves on in pure math for so long is that we’re the only subject that has absolute proof. We have certainty. We’re as close to certainty as anything that humanity can do. We can write a proof. Euclid’s proofs are still correct today, even though he wrote them in 300 BC. There’s nothing in the science or medicine of 300 BC that is still accepted, but all of the math is still true.

So there is something eternal and very special about math. Even though we’re just primates, somehow we’re tapping into something really deep. And so to say, “Well, science and engineering are the models for math,” would be a big sacrifice to the purest of pure mathematicians. They don’t want to give up the certainty that we’ve always been so proud of.

Ars: There’s a sadness among many mathematicians, not just for the epistemic questions, but also for the impact on why we do math in the first place. You write about that “aha!” moment when you’re struggling with a problem and suddenly you see the pattern. Are we losing that?

Strogatz: There’s so many things that mathematicians are in grief about, those of us who feel grief. I have been through the whole sequence of the five stages of grief. I’m joking with you a little. But the young students don’t think this is funny. I’m an old person at the end of my career, so it’s one thing for me to be philosophical about it. But imagine being 25 years old and you love this subject and you’ve dreamt about being a mathematician, and now people are saying the subject is over. There are even people gloating about it. Some of the people in the tech community are very cruel about what’s happening to math.

We talked about the epistemic aspect, but there’s also the culture of productive struggle. The pure math people like Terry Tao have been emphasizing understanding. That’s our idea of insight, that when you try hard to understand something, even if you don’t solve it, you often are so resourceful in thinking of strategies or other simplified versions of the problem. You learn a lot on the journey. You also have all this companionship and human joy of being with other people who love the thing you love. This is not restricted to math. The people who love art or weaving—my colleagues in creative writing are bereft over what their students are experiencing now, handing in AI [generated work]. They want writing with soul, with human individuality.

Ars: That is the opposite of what AI does. I guess I worry that it will do the same thing to math. There is a beauty to math, an aesthetic element. If all you’re focused on is getting the answers and ignore the journey, those are qualitative losses. Mathematicians have individual voices, too.

Strogatz: Totally. There are people whose style is very visible in the questions they ask, in the approach they take to them, in the way they explain themselves. I have cried on camera for several interviews over the past few months because there are lots of things maybe being lost. But I want to put an underline on the fact that we don’t really know. For example, what if AI gets really good at teaching us? I find when I interact with it, that it can be a very effective explainer.

And why do we have to feel sad? Maybe we can understand math better than ever with the help of this machine. We may not get to make the greatest discoveries because the machine will probably be making them, but we can still make little discoveries. I never made a great discovery. I’m not at the level of a Fields medalist, but I can still enjoy math and so can people way below me. There are recreational mathematicians who take pleasure in discovery, whatever they figure out on their own. Just like when a person solves a puzzle, it’s not like a jigsaw puzzle or Sudoku is important. You just have the pleasure of thinking.

There are people who love the workout part of it. There are people who like the competition. We shouldn’t pretend. There are people who are thrilled by the idea of being the first to make a big discovery. That’s animating for some folks, and it will be hard for them.

Strogatz: So far the AIs are not good at asking questions. I think they could be trained to ask good questions. A graduate student is often not good at asking questions when they start because in college you’re not taught to ask questions, you’re taught to give answers. The hardest thing in training a new PhD or postdoc is helping them figure out how to ask questions. I think we could do that with AIs, too.

There is a feeling of loss, but I don’t think we should shortchange the feeling of excitement. There’s so many practical, important benefits that could happen in energy technology and climate and medicine, theoretical physics, pure math. I mean, we’re making astonishing discoveries through this machine. So for a lot of people, it’s a very joyful time. It’s very confusing. That’s the only honest assessment.

We end the book with Faust. Usually people hear “Faustian bargain” as, “You have sold your soul to the devil, now you’re going to pay.” Goethe’s version is more ambiguous: that if we keep striving to build something bigger than ourselves, maybe we can be redeemed. But it’s still a very dangerous game that we have chosen to play.

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#378. Best Open Earbuds (2026): Shokz, Bose, Soundcore, and More

Open earbuds are the big new thing in headphone land. Unlike in-ear variants, open earbuds are like tiny speakers that rest on the ear and let outside sound in naturally, so you can fully hear the world around you. Some use a hook style that wraps around the back of your ear, while others are clip-ons that look more like statement-piece earrings. Style aside, they are excellent for anyone who finds traditional earbuds uncomfortable or wants full environmental awareness for activities like running, biking, or even just doing chores around the house.

I’ve tested dozens of models since 2022, and while I still recommend having a pair of noise-canceling earbuds, I also love open earbuds for specific use cases.

For more headphone recommendations, check out our guides to the Best Wireless Earbuds, Best Workout Headphones, and Best Wireless Headphones.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

These are truly take-everywhere, do-anything headphones I would recommend to anyone looking for great open earbuds. They are exceedingly comfortable and easy to use all day, so much so that I sometimes forgot I was wearing them.

They’re clip-ons that wrap around the earlobe, with the speaker end resting at the ear canal opening and the other end behind the ear. Importantly, the top of your ear is free for glasses, sunglasses, or hats. Like nearly all open earbuds, they let in sound from your surroundings, so don’t expect them to be a great companion for long-haul flights or daily gym sessions.

There are other open earbuds that are nearly as good as these, and some surpass them in areas like sound quality. But it’s a combination of small details that puts the AeroClip 2 at the top. The physical button controls on each earbud are much easier to use than touch-sensitive alternatives, especially when running or exercising outdoors. The charging case is surprisingly small, smaller than most other options on this list. And, importantly, the call quality is great. These buds use the same AI-powered chip as the Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro, and while they don’t sound quite as good, they are noticeably better than other open earbuds, especially in noisy environments.

The best part? They cost less than many similar competitors I tested.

My former top pick, and still a great option, especially if you value battery life. These earbuds do most of what the Soundcore AeroClip 2 does, just a little larger and a little pricier. The buds are exceedingly comfortable and stable for all-day wear, even during outdoor workouts.

What sets them apart from the AeroClip 2 is battery life. They are best in class—10 hours on a single charge, and 40 hours total with the charging case. They also have an IP57 dust and water-resistance rating, the same as premium, flagship earbuds like Apple AirPods Pro 3 and Samsung Galaxy Buds4 Pro. I’ve worn them in the rain, on the beach, and fully submerged them in water multiple times without issue.

They are a bit pricey, though. Shokz recently launched the lower-priced Shokz OpenDots Air and Shokz OpenFit Air 2—I may update this recommendation depending on how my testing goes.

The Bose Ultra Open Earbuds were a big deal when they launched in 2024—a brand-new design from Bose and one of the biggest swings from a major brand in clip-on open earbuds. Two years later, the brand launched the second-generation version, and they are a solid, if expensive, option. That’s mainly because of sound quality—these earbuds sound clearer and more defined than most competitors. Another differentiator is physical button controls on each bud, which I find easier to use than touch alternatives, especially when running or biking.

Like the Soundcore and Shokz earbuds, they are very comfortable, so much so that I sometimes forgot I am wearing them. This gen-two version has a more distinct, two-tone material design that is certainly eye-catching, especially in the white colorway. They also now support wireless charging, a big omission in the first generation. But they are much pricier by comparison, and only worth it if you want the best sound quality in this clip-on form factor.

It can be a little nerve-wracking to spend big bucks on a concept (open earbuds) you aren’t totally convinced by. That’s one reason I love this $50 option—the PearClip Pros aren’t super pricey and are a great way to find out if you even like open earbuds in the first place, especially the kind that clip onto the outside of your ear.

They are far less refined than Shokz or Soundcore. Things like the app and touch controls can be a little finicky. But that’s common at this super-low price point, and you can always upgrade to a more premium earbud if you fall in love with the clip-on form factor.

The Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 are more like headphones than earbuds—with a wraparound headband, long battery life, great sound quality (for open headphones), and no charging case. They use a combination of bone conduction (think vibrations) and air conduction (think tiny speakers pointed toward your ears) to deliver clearer sound than most smaller open earbuds, especially in noisy environments. That combination of technologies is why these are some of my favorite earbuds for outdoor fitness activities like running and biking.

I do wish these headphones were a little cheaper. I’m currently testing the recently released, more affordable Shokz OpenRun Air 2, and I’m hopeful they can be a budget-friendly alternative.

Apple AirPods 5 With Wireless Charging Case for $149: Apple AirPods 5 are semi-open earbuds—they still go in your ears, but don’t have rubber eartips that block outside noise, meaning you can still hear the world around you pretty clearly. Because they go in your ear somewhat, they have better sound quality and automated noise-canceling than nearly all of my top picks. Fit, however, is a big issue. While nearly all of my top picks are excellent workout companions, the AirPods 5 are quite the opposite—they can fall out often during exercise and are tricky to control mid-run.

Nothing Ear (Open) for $99: Former WIRED editor Adrienne So loves these earbuds and uses them for almost all her outdoor activities. They are very slim (19-mm wide) and lightweight. They fit slightly inside your ear and, like most Nothing headphones, have a distinct transparent design. The case doesn’t clamp shut very firmly, so be careful, but at this price, that’s forgivable.

CMF Clip Pro for $99: If you want something a little nicer and a little more comfortable than our budget pick (the Soundpeats PearClip Pro), these CMF open earbuds are a solid option. Sure, they’re a big step up in price, but for under $100, I found them more comfortable and easier to use thanks to the physical button control on each earbud (similar to my top picks).

JLab Epic Open Sport for $100: JLab’s Epic Open Sport stands out for its controls: the JLab emblem is a touch sensor, and each earbud also has physical buttons on top, making it a breeze to control. What holds the Epic Open Sport back is audio quality—the sound isn’t very detailed and is generally boring to listen to.

EarFun Clip for $70: For around $70, these are a solid pick for anyone on a budget. Former WIRED reviewer Waniata found the overall package punches above its price point, with a snappy, compact case, a comfortable fit, push-button controls, and reliable multi-device Bluetooth connections. The problem is our budget pick, the Soundpeats PearlClip Pro, often sells for less and offers a similar overall experience. Don’t dismiss these earbuds if you find them heavily discounted.

Shokz OpenFit Pro for $250: The Shokz OpenFit Pro has a great premise: open earbuds with noise canceling. Hear the world around you as you would without headphones, and turn on noise-canceling when you don’t, just like regular earbuds. And while they do cancel some noise, it’s not much. The bigger issue is price: for $250, you could get open earbuds and great noise-canceling earbuds that do a better job for each task.

Suunto Wing 2 for $179: These open-ear headphones are designed for endurance athletes—they have a long 12-hour battery life and come with a wireless power bank you can take on the go. Dock the headphones in the power bank for up to 36 hours of total battery life. There’s nothing inherently wrong with these headphones, but I don’t see a world where I would recommend them over the Shokz Openrun Pro 2, which retails for the same amount and offers more comfort, a sleeker design, better sound, and a more robust app.

Suunto Spark for $179: The Suunto Spark has a similar story to the Suunto Wing 2: it's built for athletes and syncs with Suunto fitness watches, but the similarly priced Shokz Openfit 2 outclasses it in the areas that matter (comfort, sound quality, battery).

What Are Open Earbuds and How Do They Sound?

At a glance, open earbuds seem a lot like typical wireless earbuds. The big difference is that, instead of going inside your ear canal, they rest somewhere on the outside of your ear, leaving it open so you can easily hear the world around you. I use them all the time for outdoor exercise like running or biking, where I want my music but also need to hear other runners, bikers, and cars to stay safe.

Because they leave your ears open and the sound comes from farther away (outside your ear rather than inside), audio performance isn’t as clear, intimate, or bassy as regular earbuds. They also typically lack noise-canceling features, so they are not a great fit for the office or air travel.

Open earbuds are perfect for outdoor activities or when you want to talk to other people without taking off your headphones. When I run or go for a bike ride, I only use open earbuds so I can hear my surroundings and stay safe. I also like using them around the house when I am cooking or doing laundry.

Semi-open earbuds, like Apple’s AirPods, sit inside the ear but don’t have eartips that create a sound seal. They can offer better audio quality than other open earbuds because the speakers and microphones are closer to your ear and mouth. Semi-open earbuds are comfortable, but they’re usually pretty loose—they can fall out easily and may be a poor option for fitness activities.

I test open earbuds like I test any pair of headphones: in the real world, in my daily life. I wear each pair for at least a few weeks to test comfort, battery life, ease of use, and onboard controls. I listen to podcasts, watch TV shows, jam out to my favorite playlists, and call friends.

With open earbuds in particular, I also wear them on jogs, bike rides, and errand runs to get a better feel for how stable they are on my ears. I don’t expect them to cancel any noise, so I don’t test them on airplanes or loud commutes—they aren’t really made for that. My main audio source is Spotify Lossless, but, when possible, I test other formats and codecs as well.

#377. Teenage swimmer breaks two world records in four days

Sixteen-year-old Summer McIntosh broke the world record for the 400m individual medley at the Canadian swimming trials on Saturday – just days after breaking the world record for the 400m freestyle.

McIntosh finished the 400m individual medley in a time of 4:25.87, breaking the mark set at the 2016 Rio Olympics by Hungarian swimmer Katinka Hosszú with a time of 4:26.36.

The result continues the teenager’s brilliant week after she broke the 400m freestyle world record last Tuesday – breaking defending Olympic champion Ariarne Titmus’ previous record of 3:56.40, which was set last May, in a time of 3:56.08.

Speaking after her latest triumph, McIntosh shared her emotions.

“That’s the first time I really vividly heard the crowd during my race,” McIntosh said, per Reuters.

“It’s amazing to have all my family and friends in the stands, cheering me on. It really helped me in the last 100 meters.”

The Canadian teen made her Olympic debut aged 14 at Tokyo 2020, where she finished fourth in the 200-meter freestyle.

She bagged gold in the 200m butterfly and 400m medley at the world championships in 2022, as well as two golds at the Commonwealth Games in the 200m and 400m medleys.

She now trains in Florida under coach Brent Arckey with the Sarasota Sharks team.
